Let's walk through a real booking that illustrates exactly why this redemption has earned its place in the ChooseFI community's hall of fame.

The Setup: Two Nights at the Park Hyatt Tokyo

You're planning a trip to Japan in early April — a shoulder period just after peak cherry blossom season, when the city is still spectacular but the crowds have thinned slightly. You pull up hyatt.com and find award availability at the Park Hyatt Tokyo for two nights at 25,000 points per night.

The Cash Cost: A quick search on the Park Hyatt Tokyo's direct booking page for the same dates shows standard King rooms starting at $1,100/night. For two nights, that's $2,200 in cash — before resort fees or any extras.

The Points Cost: 50,000 World of Hyatt points (25,000 × 2 nights), transferred instantly from Chase Ultimate Rewards.

The CPP Calculation: $2,200 cash value ÷ 50,000 points = 4.4 cents per point — well above the program's already-impressive baseline and squarely in the sweet spot's 2.7–6.7 cpp range.

What You Actually Experience: The Park Hyatt Tokyo occupies floors 39–52 of the Shinjuku Park Tower skyscraper. Your King Deluxe room on the 42nd floor has floor-to-ceiling windows framing the Tokyo skyline — on a clear morning, Mount Fuji appears in the distance like a postcard. The bathroom features a deep soaking tub, Aesop amenities, and heated floors. Breakfast in the Club on the 41st floor is an exquisite affair — if you hold Globalist status, it's included for both guests, adding roughly $60–$80 per person per day in value.

If you've achieved Globalist status, a complimentary suite upgrade at check-in (space available) could place you in a room with panoramic corner views that would retail for $1,800+ per night.

This is the kind of redemption that makes the FI math click in a visceral way. You earned 50,000 Chase UR points — achievable through a single premium travel card welcome bonus — and converted them into nearly $2,500 of genuine luxury. That's the system working exactly as it should.

The Park Hyatt category properties — especially Tokyo and New York — have notoriously limited award availability. The booking window opens 395 days in advance, and for high-demand dates (cherry blossom season in Japan, summer in Paris, New Year's in New York), competitive award inventory can disappear within days of opening. Set a calendar reminder for 395 days before your target date and be ready to search and transfer the same day.

The 1:1 instant transfer from Chase Ultimate Rewards makes the Chase ecosystem your most efficient pipeline into World of Hyatt. The Chase Sapphire Preferred and Chase Sapphire Reserve both transfer to Hyatt at 1:1, instantly. Pair either with the Chase Freedom Unlimited or Chase Freedom Flex to funnel everyday spending into the UR ecosystem before converting to Hyatt points when you have a target booking.

Cash prices at Park Hyatt properties fluctuate dramatically — your points cost does not. A room at the Park Hyatt Paris-Vendôme during Paris Fashion Week might run $2,000/night while your award costs the same 25,000 points as a Tuesday in November. The bigger the cash premium on your dates, the higher your effective CPP. Research when local demand spikes and target those windows deliberately.

World of Hyatt points expire after 24 months of account inactivity. This is activity-based expiration — any earning or redemption resets the clock. Don't let a large balance sit dormant. A small hotel stay, a points transfer, or earning through a Hyatt credit card all count as qualifying activity.

This is the cardinal mistake. Chase UR → Hyatt transfers are irreversible. If you transfer 60,000 points and then discover your target dates are unavailable, those points are now stranded in Hyatt — useful for Hyatt redemptions, but no longer flexible. Always confirm award space first, then transfer.

While 40,000 points/night for a Cat 8 property sounds steep, certain Park Hyatt properties in this tier — like the Park Hyatt Maldives Hadahaa — can retail for $2,000+/night, delivering CPP values that rival the best airline redemptions. Don't automatically limit your search to Category 7.

Hyatt does use peak and off-peak pricing tiers that can push Category 7 awards from 25,000 to 30,000 points on high-demand dates. Always check the actual points cost displayed during your specific date search rather than assuming the standard rate applies.

Park Hyatt is Hyatt's top-tier luxury brand, competing directly with Four Seasons, Ritz-Carlton, and Aman resorts. What makes this a travel rewards sweet spot is the disconnect between cash prices and points cost. While competitors like Marriott Bonvoy® may charge 85,000-100,000 points for comparable luxury, Hyatt keeps Park Hyatt redemptions at Category 7-8 (25,000-30,000 points). Combined with the 1:1 transfer ratio from Chase Ultimate Rewards, a single Chase Sapphire Preferred sign-up bonus can fund multiple nights of genuine luxury.

Earn Chase Ultimate Rewards through the Sapphire Preferred, Sapphire Reserve, or business cards like the Ink Preferred. A single sign-up bonus often covers 2-3 Park Hyatt nights. Alternatively, earn directly with the World of Hyatt credit card.

Log into your Chase account and transfer Ultimate Rewards to World of Hyatt at a 1:1 ratio. Transfers are typically instant, so you can transfer right before booking. Only transfer what you need for confirmed availability.

Use the World of Hyatt website or app to search your desired Park Hyatt property and dates. Filter by "Points" to see award availability. Check flexible date ranges to find the best redemption opportunities.

Complete the booking using your Hyatt points. Make sure you are logged into your World of Hyatt account so elite benefits apply. Consider booking a standard room and requesting a suite upgrade at check-in if you have Globalist status.

If you have Globalist status, contact the hotel before arrival to request suite upgrades and confirm breakfast inclusion. Even without top-tier status, joining World of Hyatt (free) earns you base-level benefits and points on incidental spend.

The fastest path is through Chase Ultimate Rewards. Cards like the Chase Sapphire Preferred and Chase Sapphire Reserve earn Ultimate Rewards that transfer 1:1 to World of Hyatt. A single sign-up bonus of 60,000-75,000 points can cover 2-3 nights at a Park Hyatt. You can also earn directly with the World of Hyatt credit card.

Compared to other luxury hotel chains, Park Hyatt availability is relatively good. Booking 3-6 months in advance for popular properties like Park Hyatt Tokyo or Park Hyatt Maldives improves your chances. Off-peak and shoulder season dates often have wide-open availability.

Yes. Globalist elite status works at all Park Hyatt properties and unlocks suite upgrades (subject to availability), free breakfast, late checkout, and waived resort fees. This dramatically increases the total value of a points stay.

Properties in high-cost destinations like Tokyo, New York, Paris, Sydney, and the Maldives typically deliver the highest cents-per-point value because their cash rates are so expensive. A Park Hyatt Tokyo stay worth $600-$800/night for 25,000 points is a standout redemption.

This redemption is purpose-built for the intentional luxury traveler in the ChooseFI community — someone who has been systematically accumulating Chase Ultimate Rewards or Bilt Rewards points and wants to convert that discipline into a genuinely extraordinary hotel experience, not just a free night at a mid-tier property.

The minimum to play: You need at least 25,000 World of Hyatt points for a single night — ideally 50,000–75,000 for a meaningful multi-night stay. This is achievable through a single Chase Sapphire welcome bonus plus modest everyday spending.

This redemption earns a **moderate difficulty rating**, and it's worth being specific about where the friction lives — because once you understand it, most of the difficulty evaporates. **The earning is easy.** Chase Ultimate Rewards points flow into World of Hyatt at 1:1 instantly, and Chase is one of the most accessible premium rewards ecosystems for new-to-intermediate travel rewards participants. The points pipeline is well-established and reliable. **The transfer and booking mechanics are easy.** The actual process — confirm availability, transfer points, complete booking — is straightforward if you follow the correct sequence. The Hyatt website is functional and the award search is transparent. **The hard part is availability.** Park Hyatt properties are genuinely popular, the award inventory is limited, and the most desirable dates (cherry blossom season, major holidays, Fashion Week) book out fast. This is where most people hit a wall — they discover the sweet spot, feel excited, and then find no availability for their dates. **Three tips to overcome the availability challenge:** 1. **Use the full 395-day booking window.** Plan further ahead than feels natural. If you want Tokyo in April of next year, you should be searching in late March or early April of the current year. 2. **Be flexible by 3–5 days on either side.** Award inventory often opens mid-week when demand is lower. Shifting from a Saturday check-in to a Thursday can unlock availability that doesn't exist on peak nights. 3. **Check repeatedly near the 30-day mark.** Properties occasionally release additional award space as the date approaches. Setting a weekly reminder to re-check your target dates costs nothing. If you're willing to plan ahead and stay flexible on exact dates, moderate difficulty becomes very manageable — and the reward on the other side is worth every bit of the effort.

This sweet spot was last verified over 90 days ago. Award availability and pricing may have changed — verify current rates before booking.

The Park Hyatt sweet spot is one of the most compelling redemptions in the entire travel rewards landscape. Booking a genuine ultra-luxury hotel experience for 25,000-30,000 points — points that transfer 1:1 from Chase Ultimate Rewards — delivers 2-4 cents per point in value. Whether it is the iconic Park Hyatt Tokyo, the beachfront Park Hyatt Maldives, or the classic Park Hyatt New York, this sweet spot consistently delivers outsized value. For anyone building a Chase Ultimate Rewards strategy, Park Hyatt should be at the top of the aspiration list.

#9071. I've found the only Apple Black Friday deals worth knowing about: iPad, MacBook, AirPods, Apple Watch

As Tim Cook used to say, Good morning! Apple Black Friday deals are underway and we will be covering them all here in our live blog. We'll share the lowest prices on iPad, MacBook, Apple Pencil and Apple Watch right here, so you don't need to go hunting across the many retailers hosting Black Friday sales. So far, our favourite offer is on the AirPods Pro 3 – down a massive 40% at Amazon US, now only $149.

We've got years of experience in Apple tech, we've used almost every product released in the last decade, and we have a forensic knowledge of who they're for, what price is actually a good deal, and advice on whether you really need the latest generation.

The M4 iPad Air only arrived in March, so $100 off could be the best price we see this Black Friday 2026. It's our go-to iPad for most people: far cheaper than the Pro, with Apple Pencil Pro support and enough power for drawing, photo editing and light Final Cut work. Prefer a larger screen? The 13-inch model has $100 off too.

This looks like a small saving, but it's the deepest price cut so far on Apple's first "budget MacBook", released in March 2026. It won't suit heavy video or 3D work, though we found it a great everyday laptop for commuting and light content creation. Our MacBook Neo review has the details.

The Apple Pencil Pro is the best stylus Apple has made, and it suits creative work well. Squeeze and barrel-roll gestures speed up tool switching, and haptics, pressure sensitivity and tilt support keep drawing accurate and natural. Hover detection and Find My are handy bonuses.

Greetings! I'm Beren, the ecom editor on Creative Bloq, and today I'll be searching for all the best deals and discounts on Apple products.

Whether you're looking for a new house tablet, need a new work laptop, or want to get the best Bluetooth audio on the go, this is the right place to be.

And to kick things off – here's the best deal on the iconic MacBook Air M1. It's a renewed model, and it's £470, but I wanted to get it out there that I love this thing - it's the best laptop Apple has made in years, and if you're looking for a second lappy or something for light work, this is still an excellent, beautifully designed thing... more modern deals loading!

2020 retro laptops are good and well, but if you're looking for an up to date option, I think the M5 MacBook Air is pretty unbeatable, for most users.

It's the MacBook that I moved onto from the M1, and the bump up in speed is pretty noticeable. As with my M1, I went for a 13-inch model, as that's the perfect size for taking it to and from work in my bag. The screen is also a standout feature, and at 500 nits brightness, it's what I need to do the odd bit of photo editing, whether in a dark room or out in a bright cafe.

Right now it's down from £1,299 to £1,149 over at Amazon.

I've recently been immersed in the old school world of high end audio – especially wired earphones and headphones. And there's an uncomfortable truth that many in the hobby don't want to admit – Bluetooth audio can be just as good!

Of course, it's often not, because most commercial earphones are tuned with insane amounts of bass and treble (a V-shape tuning), missing those finer details in the midrange that audiophiles love so much. But now and again there's a wireless set that really jumps out.

In audiophile circles, that set is the Apple AirPods Pro 2.

Because they have been superseded by the third iteration, you'll only find them sold as renewed models, but I would recommend anyone who is even slightly serious about audio to seek a pair out before they disappear altogether.

You can get a pair of the AirPods Pro 2 for £137.89 over at Amazon.

It might not be the most popular view at my work, but... why do most people buy the iPad Pro?!

Yes, it's an incredibly powerful tablet that can be integrated into a video editing workflow... but how many of you reading this are video editors? And how many of those are realistically going to spend over a grand to bring a little bit of portability to your set up, when laptops exist?!

For the vast majority of users – including creative professionals – I think the iPad Air, and even the classic iPad in some circumstances, will do the job just fine. Which is just as well, as they are noticeably cheaper than the Pro.

I've used them all extensively, and for me the classic iPad does what a good tablet should do, and then some. I'd pick up the Air if you wanted to take your mobile gaming a little more serious, or if you're venturing into photo editing and film watching... but really the entry level iPad does all of that just fine.

Right now you can buy the classic 11-inch iPad down from £429 to £399 over at Amazon.

It's confession time: I don't really get the Apple Watch. Never have. I've tried to use one on several occasions. But it always ended up slipping off my wrist and sitting patiently in a draw, waiting my next seasonal exploration into health-based activities.

But I hear that people – fitter, happier, more productive people than I – love them, and I know a good deal when I see it.

You can get the Apple Watch SE 3 GPS 44mm over at Amazon for £223, down from £249.

Possibly an Apple deal that will get overlooked this Black Friday is the current 50% off Apple TV.

The deal is you pay $6.99 for the first six months, and then $14.99 thereafter... or you could always cancel.

It's one of those deals that will be completely dependant on what shows they've currently got on their roster. For me, Slow Horses may be the deciding factor!

Bringing some clarity to a 'deal' on the iPhone Air that I've seen doing the rounds.

I've seen some sites calling the current price of £799 on the 256GB iPhone Air the latest discount. But it's not. Although the Air went on sale at £999 back in September 2025, earlier this year it settled at its new £799 price pretty much everywhere, largely due to push back from Apple fans at the slightly outrageous price tag.

Don't get me wrong – we love the design of the iPhone Air. But we also want to be as transparent as possible with Creative Bloq readers. This is a good phone, but its £799 price is not a Black Friday deal. We'll tell you as soon as it gets one.

Unfortunately, one Apple product you won't see me recommend – no matter how good the deal – is the AirPods Max.

As we detailed in our review, entitled, Obviously good, near-impossible to recommend, both generations of the Max are problematic for several reasons, and it's all totally avoidable.

The main issue, though it's certainly not the only one, is the price. At £500, with fierce competition cheaper, it's just a really hard sell. The tuning isn't so amazing to justify the price, and then you've got the 386g weight, the lack of EQ, and that very, very strange nappy/bra 'case'. Oh, and there's no off and on switch.

And this has been the case since its 2020 launch!

Honestly, I would go for the deal on the AirPods Pro instead. At £189, down from £219 over at John Lewis, it's a far better audio option.

Hiya! It's Georgia here, editor of CB and – as someone who is firmly trapped in the Apple ecosystem – I've got all the knowledge you need to help you make a firm decision on the purchases you make this week.

So far, my standout deal is on the AirPods Pro 3. I use these earbuds everyday, and I have been impressed by the sound quality, fit and the amazing noise cancellation.

I can't believe that these have dropped under $150 from $149 at Amazon. The deal isn't quite so good in the UK, but it is £165.99, which is still a decent discount down from the RRP of £250.

So, as we know, Apple make a range of laptops suitable for all different types of users. If you're not in the know with the laptop models, here's an explainer.

MacBook Air is Apple's super slim, light and powerful option. Every iteration gets supercharged, and it becomes harder to choose between the Air and the Pro each year. The Air works best for light to medium creative workflows - photo and light video editing and graphic design works perfectly on the Air. It's also a bit cheaper than the Pro. Read our MacBook Air M5 review.

This is the beast that works best for heavy users – think 3D workflows and heavy video editing tasks. Obviously it comes in a multitude of iterations, with the top level of power serving creative professionals working on intensive projects. See our MacBook Pro M4 review.

MacBook Neo is the newest laptop on the block. Built to rival a Chromebook, it's best for casual users who want a laptop that can manage the basics. It can still deal with some very light creative tasks. See our MacBook Neo review.

You'll find deals on all these laptops this week.

Apple started out using Intel's chips, but began making its own in 2020. The naming convention is pretty simple – the chips are numbered, in order, and the number is precluded by an 'M'. So 2020 saw the M1 chip, and we're now at the M5. There have been significant jumps in performance since then, but that doesn't mean everyone needs the latest chip. You may well find the level of power you're looking for in an older model – I'm still using the M2 MacBook Air, for example, and it's plenty powerful enough for everything I use it for.

#9070. CLB Architects creates ADU in Wyoming with rock-climbing wall

US studio CLB Architects has completed an accessory dwelling unit called Wiley, which features an outdoor climbing wall and compact living quarters for an empty-nester couple.

The small building stands on a one-acre site in Wilson, Wyoming, located just beyond the popular ski town of Jackson. The site is dotted with mature trees and sits along the west bank of the Snake River.

Before the project’s inception, the clients had lived on the property for 25 years – in a modest, 1960s house they had renovated – and had raised their son there.

As their son neared graduation from high school, the couple decided to build an ADU on the property and make it their full-time residence, while renting out the main residence.

“The new house would allow them to remain on the land they had known for decades, while experiencing it in a new way – closer to nature, with stronger connections to light, views and outdoor living,” said Jackson-based CLB Architects.

The house also represents a way to accommodate a growing need for housing while preserving the natural landscape.

“In our region, there’s a clear need for this housing type, which is economical, compact and responsive to place,” said CLB Architects partner Eric Logan.

A primary challenge for the design team was to ensure the house “met the couple’s programmatic and budget constraints” within a very compact footprint. Per country regulations, the new house could not exceed 1,000 square feet (92.9 square metres).

The architects conceived a simple, rectangular volume that rises two levels and is topped with a gabled roof. The house was carefully sited so it would feel separate from the main residence.

“Siting the building toward the back of the parcel and introducing new landscaping and tree plantings created a soft buffer between the two dwellings,” the architect said.

The team carved out portions of the exterior to form inset terraces, along with a climbing wall that is used by the couple’s son while home from college. On the east-facing elevation, a boxy protrusion forms a balcony.

Both inside and out, the team opted for materials that were durable, cost-efficient and complemented the building’s form. Dark corrugated metal clads most of the building, while tight-knot cedar was used for inset areas to provide “warmth and depth”.

The ground level contains a spacious garage for vehicles and outdoor gear. The upper level holds two bedrooms with ensuite bathrooms, all of which are organised around a central living area.

“Locating the main living spaces on the second floor allows the interiors to engage the tree canopy while maximising natural light, offering a more intimate relationship with the landscape,” the team said.

The living area opens onto a west-facing deck, which acts as an “outdoor living room” for much of the year. Large, sliding glass doors diminish the boundary between inside and out and usher in breezes during summer months.

The clients, both of whom have deep experience in design and construction fields, poured themselves into the project. The husband served as the general contractor and engaged local tradespeople to help out.

“A true labor of love, the couple built much of the house themselves, working on the construction every evening and on weekends,” the team said, noting the project was completed in about nine months.

The project offers ideas for how communities in the Mountain West can accommodate growth while preserving the natural landscape.

“With rising land values and the need to accommodate more residents, homes like this – that are compact, efficient, and contextual – can provide more housing while preserving open space,” the team said.

“As local communities grapple with growth, projects like this suggest one path forward.”

Other ADUs in America include a small, cedar-clad dwelling in California’s wine country by Schwartz and Architecture, and a compact, metal-clad building in Austin by North Arrow Studio that resembles a birdhouse.

#9069. From the margins to the mainstream: the growing market for illustration art

Norman Rockwell’s Home on Leave (1945) © Norman Rockwell

The illustration art market began in the 1960s when, according to Roger Reed, a Manhattan-based independent art dealer in this field, works used in children’s storybooks, product advertising and magazine covers “were taken out of their context in publishing and sold just as paintings”. Some six decades later and the apotheosis of that market has arrived with the recent opening of the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art in Los Angeles, the $1bn creation of film-maker George Lucas (Star Wars and Indiana Jones) devoted to children’s book art, fantasy art, cartoon images, movie posters, film stills and magazine illustrations, as well as works distinguished as fine art by the likes of Paul Cadmus, Diego Rivera and Carrie Mae Weems.

Lucas and fellow filmmaker Steven Spielberg have been some of the largest collectors of the original art created by illustrators for decades, but many others have caught up. Today, the interest in works by Norman Rockwell, N.C. Wyeth, J.C. Leyendecker, Howard Pyle, Maxfield Parrish, Jessie Willcox Smith, John Held Jr and Charles Dana Gibson, among many others, has mushroomed—and in some cases prices have shot up from almost zero to millions of dollars.

“A lot of the work of illustrators was pooh-poohed by the art world, because they were illustrators,” says the New York-based American art dealer Debra Force, “but you don’t hear that so much anymore.”

Certainly, one doesn’t hear that at the major auction houses where works by Rockwell, Parrish, Wyeth and Leyendecker frequently bring the highest prices in American art sales. Norman Rockwell (1894-1978) leads the pack, with his 1951 painting for a Saturday Evening Post cover, Saying Grace, fetching $46m at a 2013 Sotheby’s auction and his 1957 oil painting The Rookie (Red Sox Locker Room) sold for $22.5m at a 2014 auction at Christie’s. The 1922 painting Daybreak by Maxfield Parrish(1870-1966) earned $7.6m at a Christie’s sale in 2006, while a 1943 tempera on panel, Portrait of a Farmer, by N.C. Wyeth (1882-1945) brought $5.9m at Sotheby’s in 2018. Football Hero, the 1914 painting for a Saturday Evening Post cover by J.C. Leyendecker (1874-1951), brought $4.1m at a Heritage Auctions sale in 2021, and the 1907 painting Captain Keitt by Howard Pyle (1853-1911) for the frontispiece of his novel The Ruby of Kishmoor earned $702,000 at a 2004 sale at Sotheby’s.

“There’s definitely a hierarchy,” says Aviva Lehmann, the deputy chair of fine art at Heritage Auctions, which sold Rockwell’s 1943 work So You Want to See the President! in 2025 to the White House Historical Association for $7.2m.

However, “Rockwell’s success has not been at the expense of these other illustrators”, says Skye Lacerte, an illustration art specialist at Swann Auction Galleries in New York. “Rather, it has helped establish a broader market in which collectors and museums are beginning to take the entire field seriously.” She notes that “immediately recognisable” images from magazine covers and illustrations from famous books like Alice in Wonderland, The Wind in the Willows, or L. Frank Baum’s Oz books are highly sought after, as well as advertising art for “companies like Coca-Cola, TWA and Cadillac because those images have become part of American cultural experience”.

Besides the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art, there is the Brandywine River Museum of Art in Chadds Ford, Pennsylvania; the Norman Rockwell Museum in Stockbridge, Massachusetts; the Eric Carle Museum of Picture Book Art in Amherst, Massachusetts; and the National Museum of American Illustration in Newport, Rhode Island. That last museum was founded in 1998 by Judy Goffman Cutler, the owner of Manhattan’s American Illustrators Gallery, who claims to have sold Lucas “hundreds” of original paintings by the top book and magazine illustrators. “I sold him his first Rockwell—it was called Going Out,” she says—a 1933 painting that was used on the cover of the Saturday Evening Post. For reasons of “client confidentiality”, she declines to say how many works in the illustration field she has sold to Lucas, only noting that “I built his collection”.

Other museums that aren’t wholly devoted to illustration or storytelling art also have collections of this type of work, most notably the New Britain Museum of American Art in Connecticut and the Delaware Art Museum in Wilmington. The New Britain Museum has almost 1,800 works in its Sanford B.D. Low Illustration Collection, named in honour of the institution’s first director who himself had been an illustrator and invited illustrators he knew to donate works for a collection. They include such artists as Willcox Smith, Everett Raymond Kinstler, Stevan Dohanos, Walter Wick and William Steig.

“Interest in illustration art doesn’t begin and end with Rockwell, and the awareness of illustration art as art is definitely increasing,” says Lisa Williams, head of curatorial affairs at the New Britain Museum.

N.C. Wyeth’s Victory Garden (1943) © N.C. Wyeth

Others agree. “I have no doubt that the collective appreciation for the category will continue to grow thanks to its elevation by these museums,” says Quincie Dixon, head of sale in Christie’s American art department. She adds that “private collectors make up the bulk of this market, but perhaps that will change now that there are museums on both coasts dedicated to the category”.

Specialised museums and collections reflect a growing prominence, but they might also be keeping these works segregated. Goffman Cutler states that it is her “goal to have museums include American illustration art in their American art galleries”, which the occasional museum has done, but not many and not too often.

A spokesperson for the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, notes that the “collection includes art from American artists of many backgrounds, including quite a few who have worked as illustrators, among them Winslow Homer, Childe Hassam, William Glackens, Joseph Leyendecker, Charles Sheeler” and some others. Having worked as illustrators doesn’t mean that their illustration work is what the museum shows, and the Leyendecker is not currently “on view”. Both New York’s Metropolitan Museum of Art and the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, own paintings by Parrish that are not displayed in their American art galleries, but the Art Institute of Chicago has hung its Rockwell, The Dugout (1948), in one of the Arts of Americas galleries, and the Crystal Bridges Museum of American Art in Bentonville, Arkansas, has hung Rockwell’s 1943 work Rosie the Riveter (which the museum purchased from a private collector in 2009) next to Charles Willson Peale’s George Washington (around 1780-82) and works by John Singleton Copley and James Peale Sr in its Visions of America galleries. “In the same section of the gallery as Rosie the Riveter,” says a museum spokesperson, “are Susie J. Lee’s Johnny [2013], Kerry James Marshall’s Our Town [1995] and a new commission by artist Teri Greeves.”

It seems the greatest test for illustration art is no longer garnering record prices, but if it can enter—and hold its own within— the art historical canon.

The Lucas Museum of Narrative Art’s new admission and membership fees are tone-deaf and self-defeating

The Star Wars director, appearing at the famed conference for the first time, described the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art as “a temple to the people’s art”

While the swooping building is impressive and easy to navigate, the collection is patchy and the displays are at times “bizarre”

After almost a decade of delays and controversies, George Lucas and Mellody Hobson launch a giant space to house a 40,000-piece collection spanning from comics to Star Wars materials to a Frida Kahlo self-portrait

#9068. The best headphone in the world just got an upgrade – but is the new HEDD DX just a warmer D1?

The HEDDphone DX is an open-back headphone that builds on the incredibly popular HEDDphone D1. It has more sub-bass and a more spiky treble, and that's a double-edged sword. Everyone will appreciate its more confident design and its improved comfort, thanks to a new Capra-created headband. But when it comes to tuning, the DX is a softer, warmer take on the lean, mean neutral D1, and I expect that'll enrage as many as it'll delight. For me, the DX is an exciting, musical set that swaps a little detail and imaging for a more fun sound. But at $400 more than the D1, and with a new Capra-created headband released for the D1 early next year, the DX runs the risk of remaining in its older sibling's shadow.

Why you can trust Creative Bloq Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.

In the world of audiophile headphones and in-ear monitors (IEMs), second generations of popular products are thick on the ground. Last year the divisive Grell OAE was followed with the far better-received Grell OAE 2. Last month the ground-breaking Kiwi Ears KE4 got a second iteration.

Price: $1,199 / £999Release: 24 November 2026Driver & housing: 50mm dynamic driver with thin-ply carbon diaphragm (TPCD); open-backMaterial: Polymer and metal chassis, soft fabric suspension strap, replaceable velour ear padsCable: Detachable dual-sided 3.5 mm ear cup connectors; textile-sleeved cables terminated in 3.5 mm (with screw-on 6.35 mm adapter) and 4.4 mm balancedImpedance: 32 Ω (at 1kHz)Sensitivity: 100dB @ 1mWWeight: 310g

So it would be simple to think of the new HEDDphone DX as take two of the best-selling (and my favourite open-back headphone) HEDDphone D1. Simple, but wrong.

HEDD have described it as 'the musical D1', but I think they're playing a risky game. Yes, they took on feedback from their audience, some of whom thought the D1 was a little lean and a touch too clean (not I, for the record). And they also took note of critics of the D1's unforgiving headband (yeah, that thing sucks). But instead of giving us a second take of the D1, I think they've tried to give us the HD 650 to the D1's HD 600. If that was the plan, I don't think they achieved it – but it's a fantastic failure nonetheless.

Big picture: If I were reviewing the HEDDphone DX purely on its tuning, design and comfort, it would be an easy recommendation to all. But the DX costs $400 more than the D1, so it becomes more complicated. To muddy the water further, this January HEDD plans to release the excellent DX headband as a $100 add on for the D1. That will make the D1 far more appealing – and still $300 cheaper than the DX!

So, there's plenty to consider when evaluating the new HEDDphone DX. One thing's for certain: The top spots of my list of the best-sounding wired headphones run the risk of being cluttered with HEDDphones.

Overall, the HEDDphone DX is an exciting, warm open-sounding set, with a very well extended lower frequency, and an immersive midrange. With that lower touch of warmth, it loses much of the crystal clarity of the D1, and some of that higher-end detail. But I still hear a spacious presentation with above-average imaging (the perceived placement of instruments), and enough of what makes the D1 great but with a whopping amount of sub-bass.

HEDD shared a B&K 5128 measurement of the DX with me (above), and it largely replicates what I hear. I definitely hear that slight recession in the 1-2kHz region, and an elevation in 3.5kHz. But for me, the treble's squiggly lines differ ever so slightly (all detailed below). What's clear is that HEDD want the DX to walk the tightrope of warmth and richness, while offering relaxed higher frequencies that give us detail without getting sibilant. And they nail it.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

This tuning suits diverse music genres and immersive gaming sessions, delivering clean transient speed, rich tonal body, and fatigue-free playback across dense, complex, layered multi-track studio recordings. I absolutely love it for EDM, but it's not peerless when it comes to vocal tracks, as we will see in the competition section below.

Bass: Most open-back dynamic headphones suffer from sub-bass roll-off, and that's generally been seen as a tradeoff for all that open, expansive presentation of music. The DX holds full sub-bass extension to 20Hz, smack in the middle of the new Headphones.com preference bounds on B&K 5128 measurements.

Warmth between 100Hz and 250Hz reaches the upper edge of that preference band, adding body and fullness to bass guitars and kick drums. According to HEDD's literature, the high-excursion carbon driver moves air with low - basically zero – distortion, meaning we get clean separation in the bass during complex musical passages.

Now, I don't really know how much of that is audible to the human ear. What I do know is that the bass is about as big and fun as I can enjoy before things start getting claustrophobic. You see, when bass gets overbearing, lower mids in particular can get swamped by it, and a lot of subtlety is lost. However, what the DX does to combat this is add a treble elevation around 10.5kHz, keeping things from getting too swampy. What you get is a big, detailed, but not bloated bass.

It's a tightrope, but the DX does a fantastic job walking it.

Midrange: With its bombastic bass and sneaky treble (more on that later), the mids of the DX are not really the star of the show. Not at first, at least.

But there's plenty going on. From 300Hz to 1kHz, the lower midrange sounds correct, not coloured, giving vocals, and string instruments solid weight. Then things get fun. Around 1.5 kHz there's a dip that comes across as relaxed, then a spike around 3.4kHz for me, which is only emphasised more due to the following dip around 5kHz.

All of which is to say, I can really crank the volume with the DX, and the upper midrange doesn't punish me for it. There's no shoutiness, and instead I get fatigue-free listening with coherent vocal articulation that's proportional against the rich low-end. What's more surprising, considering this rollercoaster, is that the timbre of the DX is natural sounding.

For my HEDD DX review I played them through the Luxsin X8 and the Chord Mojo 2 DAC/Amps. These pairings provided ample power delivery and headroom for the headphones, maintaining an uncoloured signal path from source to transducer. Music streamed via Spotify Lossless.

Treble is largely relaxed with the DX, trading sharp brightness for a smooth, fatigue-free approach. I hear reduced energy at 7kHz that lowers sibilance on a brightly mixed track like Sweet Old World by Lucinda Williams. That's not to say there's no bite here, but it never gets in the way of the music.

Though HEDD's B&K 5128 graph shows a narrow peak at 9-10kHz from their test pinna, for me I got clean treble extension without any glare. Strings, hi-hats, and room ambience retain a crisp texture over longer listening sessions.

I definitely got a bit of spice around 12 kHz, which isn't punishing, but brings with it some micro details, including the mouth clicks of female singers, as with Erykah Badu's Other Side of the Game.

To call the HEDDphone DX's treble dark is totally wrong. It's balanced, but edges towards modest rather than bright, and I think it'll be enjoyable to a lot of people.

I think the asking price of the HEDDphone DX is a hard sell. Yours for $1,199/£999, the DX enters a crowded open-back tier, and though I think it does well against many of them, thanks to its excellent German assembly, full part replaceability, and a five-year warranty, I think people will be expecting a truly exotic tuning for that price. That's not what the DX is about.

The HEDD DX matches the planar Audeze LCD-X at $1,199 but at half the weight, measuring 310g. It undercuts the Aune AR9000 ($1,399), HIFIMAN Arya Unveiled ($1,449), Focal Clear MG Pro ($1,490), and Sennheiser HD 800s ($1,999.95), but of course we're talking about a lot of different tunings there.

I think one of its strengths is its chic German design, and its matte black and subtle cream white does a lot to make it stand out from the crowd. The comfort is something many of the heavier contenders could learn from.

I think because the DX is not going for a risky, exotic tuning – which wins over fewer yet more ardent fans – it makes sense to compare it in detail to two mainstream, best-selling alternatives: The HEDD D1 and Sennheiser HD 650.

For those that missed it, HEDD shook the audiophile world last November with the release of the exquisitely-tuned HEDDphone D1. It was neutral, it was balanced, and for me it didn't seem to have any weaknesses at all. It wasn't warm, but it didn't come across as overly bright. It was about as lean as I can take it before things start sounding cold and clinical. But there was something about its tonal balance where its neutrality came across as rich (though I'd usually use that word to describe warmer sets). It remains my favourite over-ear, open-back headphone to date.

So, the HEDDphone DX has big shoes to fill. But ultimately, comparing them is like pitting Converse against DMs. They're trying to achieve different things... and yet, since they're coming from the same company, and at very different prices, I think the comparison is required.

The D1 is about clarity without exaggerating any part of the mix. The DX is about a good time – whacking up the bass, cranking up that 10.6kHz region to balance it... basically giving you one of the more refined V-shaped sound signatures in a high end pair of headphones.

Of course they share the same DNA when it comes to design and technology. Both headphones share thin-ply carbon drivers, though as said, HEDD positions the DX as "the experience" and the D1 as "the analyst". But that framing understates the musicality of the D1, which remains immersive and engaging despite its neutral focus.

In practice, the DX adds sub-bass weight, upper-bass warmth, a wider soundstage, and a spike up in the treble, whereas the D1 offers tighter bass and overall more focus. Then there's the price. The 'Refreshed' D1, with the new DX headband and travel case, will sell for $899/£699 in January, while the DX costs $1,199/£999.

For my tastes, and considering the price difference, the D1 remains the one I'd recommend to most people. It has more detail, and due to its neutrality presents music as a massive landscape of sound. The DX is more engaging with its bass and 10kHz shot in the arm, but it's still in its bigger brother's shadow.

However, if you find the D1 too lean, the DX could be what you want.

Both headphones share a warm-leaning, relaxed, largely fatigue-free tuning, but even though it feels neat to make a comparison between the D1 and DX with the HD 600 and HD 650, they're all actually slightly different headphones, with distinct tunings.

The Sennheiser HD 650's sub-bass rolls off from around 90Hz, and even though I think the HD 650's punchy mid-bass is criminally understated by critics, it's still easy to see someone wanting more sub bass than it offers. That's exactly what the HEDD DX does – a sub bass that extends deep to 20Hz.

Their midrange presentations are highlights for both headphones, though in subtly different ways. Both offer rich and realistic-sounding vocals and instruments, but I think the HD 650 offers slightly more forward, honeyed vocals, offering more around the 1-2kHz region than the DX, and less around 2.5kHz, giving a sense of space compared to the DX. The timbre of the HD 650 is pretty unbeatable, but the DX gives it a valiant effort.

The HD 650 is more heavy handed with the upper frequencies, which helps bring texture and grip to the mid-bass that it offers, whereas the DX takes a tamer approach to this region. For me, that makes the DX sound a touch soft, and less striking than the HD 650.

And so, I feel like the DX is actually somewhere in between the HD 600 and 650, rather than neatly comparing directly with the latter.

Though I don't believe it has any impact on the sound profile, it's still worth thinking of the different power needs. The 32ohm DX will run off anything, while the 300ohm HD 650 requires dedicated desktop amplification. Weighing 260g and costing around $500, the HD 650 also remains far more accessible, compared to the still-light 310g but slightly eye-watering $1,199, of the DX. Of course, you have to factor in the far superior build of the DX to the plastic fantastic HD 650.

If you're not going to miss the sub-bass, I'd still recommend the HD 650 over the DX. It's still my favourite out of the two. But if you know the HD 650 has a little too much spice in the upper frequencies, and you're after a soft, rich midrange – and you're willing to pay over twice the price – the HEDD DX should be on your radar.

Rated at 32ohms with a sensitivity of 100dB at 1mW, the DX is super easy to drive. I had no issues running it on my Fosi Audio DS2 dongle DAC.

Looking at price point brethren, unlike the 300ohm Sennheiser HD 800 S or the 94dB HIFIMAN Arya Unveiled, it reaches comfortable listening levels from such portable dongles and modest desktop units. A clean solid-state DAC and amplifier with low output impedance gives you excellent driver control, keeping the DX's elevated sub-bass articulate even during dynamic peaks.

The HEDDphone DX gets 10/10 for build and comfort. It really does excel in these areas, and I feel that this should be the new standard at this price point.

At 310g, it undercuts most rivals in its price point on weight. A built-in soft, silky suspension strap, designed by the king of headband comfort Capra Audio, is as good as it gets, distributing the weight across your head. We also get updated, super soft velour ear pads.

Clamp force feels firm on initial wear and may bother listeners sensitive to that, though it was fine for me across many hours of music and gaming sessions.

I also love the subtle matte charcoal metal finish, and updated indented metal mesh around the outer-ear. Add to that subtle white patterns on the outer-ear, making the HEDD logo come through, and you've got a very pretty pair of headphones here.

For $1,199, I'm glad that the DX comes with modular, user-replaceable parts and a five-year warranty. If the tuning is for you, you can expect this headphone to bring you joy for many, many years to come. Excellent work HEDD!

If you've read this review in full, you'll know it's no puff piece – I've made it clear where I think the HEDD DX is lacking. For example, it's less rich and detailed than the cheaper D1. Its above average timbre still doesn't compete with Sennheiser's HD 650, 20 years its senior and a third of its cost. For a sophisticated V-shape tuning, I think its $1,199/£999 price is steep and confusing.

So why 4.5 stars out of 5? Because the two headphones I've compared to the DX are two of my favourite headphones, and as close to perfect as I've heard.

Taken by itself, I think the DX offers exquisite build and comfort, and sounds fantastic. That half star deduction is because of its price. It's priced so much higher than the (in my opinion) better D1. That's confusing to me. Make them the same price, at least! Make it competitive, HEDD!

If you prefer a little bit more warmth, a far more forceful lower end and less overall clarity up top, then I could imagine that you'd prefer the DX to the D1. But until the HEDDphone DX dips under $1,000, I'm going to find it hard to recommend over the D1.

Beren cut his teeth as Staff Writer on digital art magazine ImagineFX, and has since worked on and edited several creative titles, including Paint & Draw and Computer Arts. A table lamp comprising a plastic base topped with five magnetically attached glowing orbs is among the products recently published on our Showroom section.

Magnetic connector points are placed inside the five globe-like bulbs that light this table lamp by Hong Kong-based Canalside Studio.

The Bubbly lamp comprises a statuesque base with five bulbs attached, which can be removed and positioned around a room – including attached to metal surfaces – to spread out its ambient glow.

Other products published last week include a tile collection by Ceramiche Keope, acoustic pods by Actiu and an outdoor rug range by Rima Dain.

Read on to find out about some of our latest products:

Grace Lithos tiles by Ceramiche Keope are intended to mimic the striated appearance of natural Villeneuve quartzite quarried in Italy.

As well as being striped with differently coloured striations, the tiles feature the stone’s abundance of mineral inclusions and the glinting mica microcrystals that it is studded with.

Amber and white veining streaks across the surface of Italian stone company Antolini‘s aptly-named Blueroots marble.

The slabs can be used in kitchens and bathrooms as interior cladding or to create furnishings, imbuing interiors with visually stimulating surfaces.

Office furniture brand Actiu has evolved its Qyos acoustic pods, expanding on its configuration options and capacity for personalisation.

Italian company Ceramiche Refin‘s latest surface draws on the faceted appearance of traditional terrazzo.

Palladia comes in a trio of colourways – Iride, Luce and Aurea – and a choice of two finishes, glossy Lucida or plain Matt.

Office brand Mute‘s Jetson acoustic pods have evolved to encompass a wider range of colourways, wall layouts and levels of transparency.

Also enhanced is the pods’ acoustic credentials, which the brand says now meets Class A acoustic standards in accordance with ISO 23351-1, allowing individuals and small groups to work and converse in a quiet environment.

A range of styles, shapes and sizes are available in the catalogue of Spanish brand Rima Dain, which specialises in outdoor rugs.

Rather than being an afterthought, the rugs aim to help zone and enhance outdoor spaces in both residential and hospitality contexts.

Enhanced and cutting-edge new features aim to make Swedish brand Asko‘s Steel Seal washing machines more seamless, hygienic and pleasant to use.

Two new signature technologies in particular feature in the new machines. Steel Seal, which substitutes rubber components for ones made of steel, and Quattro Construction 2.0, an integrated suspension system that reduces movement and resulting noise when in use.

Finnish company Framery has released an internal layout option for its One Pod, featuring a corner sofa in miniature.

One Lounge aims to make users feel at home with the cosy, thickly-padded corner seat, in place of a harder stool.

Bonfire Studios' Nate Bowden on putting pink into dark fantasy and designing characters you can recognise mid-battle.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A lot is going on in Arkheron. Bonfire Studios' competitive multiplayer game drops players into a dark fantasy world where teams battle through an ever-changing Tower, collecting equipment and abilities as they fight. It's fast and chaotic, which creates a challenge for the art direction: how do you make a game look beautiful when players barely have time to take in what's on screen?

Built in Unity, Arkheron answers by putting gameplay at the centre of its visual identity. That has shaped the rotating isometric camera, the colourful character designs, and how weapons, animation, and sound communicate information during combat.

I spoke to Nate Bowden, art director at Bonfire Studios, about Arkheron's world, its characters and the visual language that holds them together.

Asked for the first image that made the team feel "this is Arkheron", Bowden doesn't offer one. "I don't know if there was a single piece of art that suddenly made everything click for everyone all at once," he says. "I think Arkheron's visual identity has been something we've discovered and refined over time."

The look grew up alongside the mechanics. "The IP and its look and feel started in parallel with 'finding the fun' in its gameplay and design," he says. "Once the Arkheron that we know and love now started to take shape, art followed suit, and the team started making choices that enhanced the gameplay experience rather than just looked cool for its own sake."

If he had to name a single visual idea, it would be the camera. "It would have to be the camera and the choice to make it isometric and also one that rotated around the player," he says. "That helped inform so many decisions on where we should put time and effort."

It also shaped how the team approached dark fantasy. "I think there's a misconception that dark fantasy has to be relentlessly dark, grim, or oppressive," Bowden says. One of the team's guiding ideas has been a world that's "hauntingly beautiful", and he thinks they've shown that "you can have environments and characters that have a broad palette of colours and still feel melancholic, mysterious, and dangerous."

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

For another game that resists photorealism, read how Blades of Fire flew in the face of modern video game aesthetics, taking a painterly, high-contrast route.

His example is the rework of Dahla, the game's deadly dancer. The Eternals at the time already resembled today's lineup, but their designs were more detailed, and the palettes were, in his words, "very clamped and constrained". Then came the challenge. "The challenge I put in front of the team was 'we are going to have pink in the game.'"

"In the end I believe that she turned out not only more vibrant and colourful, but also even more threatening than her original design, which tended to disappear in the shadows," he says. The wider cast now has a broad range of colours, and the payoff is practical. "When you are in those crazy fights, it is so much easier to differentiate the characters from one another from colour alone."

"Oh man, I could answer this question forever," reflects Bowden when the focus turns to the story behind the Tower.

The short version: the Tower is an afterlife inhabited by Echoes, entities that were once human in the living world. They're trapped in an endless cycle by their own unfinished business, as the Tower builds itself up and then essentially resets. Everything in Arkheron, from someone's appearance to a piece of furniture, is formed from someone's memory, and none of it needs to be accurate. "They're imperfect recollections, shaped by emotion, experience; all rooted in that unfinished business," he says.

A type of Echo called Builders creates the levels. "Their memories and unfinished business are so strong and profound that they have, in a way, contaminated the tower architecturally."

"We want the world to feel like it has a history, even when you don't fully understand that history when you begin," Bowden says. Their stories will be revealed as people play, "which is something we can't wait to share."

Building maps that work as both fantasy spaces and competitive arenas can be difficult, but Bowden is direct in how the art team approached it. "One of the principles I feel most strongly about is that gameplay has to come first. We can create the most beautiful environment imaginable, but if it makes the game harder to understand or less enjoyable to play, we haven't done our job as developers."

The camera can orbit the action, and players are often fighting several opponents, so they need to read their surroundings almost instantly. That means thinking about silhouettes, landmarks, navigable space and how much visual information players are being asked to process. Bowden doesn't see those as limits. "Quite the opposite; they force us to make stronger decisions."

Where Arkheron's character work puts its emphasis surprised me. "A lot more emphasis is ultimately put on the items vs. the character's bodies themselves," Bowden says. "That's not to say that we don't put a lot of love and attention there too, but as a player it's more important that you quickly recognise what that enemy player has equipped, because that's 100% going to impact how you respond in combat."

So the items get every tool the team has. "Yes, of course we think about colour and shape, but we really live and die by the emphasis we put on bespoke audio, animation, and VFX." He gives three examples:

"I can literally hear you from offscreen and know when you have switched to Ravah's Crossbow. When you attack with Dahla's weapons, you move like a dancer because you are embodying her with her items. When you use Karriv's abilities, you are literally setting the playspace on fire."

The characters themselves have to work at two scales. Up close, they should be "beautiful, detailed, and full of personality". In play, they're seen from an elevated camera, surrounded by other players, abilities and effects. "At that distance, a lot of traditional character detail simply disappears. What remains is silhouette, proportion, movement, sound, and colour," he says. Because players can combine equipment and abilities in different ways, "we're not just designing a fixed cast of characters. We're creating a visual language that helps players understand what they're encountering."

When thinking about the creative process, Bowden uses the Eternals as an example, whose items are driven by gameplay. New ones usually start from a fun gameplay prototype. Sometimes the trigger is a narrative need, and sometimes it's a drawing from the skin design process that "we all just agree needs to be flushed out and developed as an Eternal."

A small group works out what's missing. If the starting point is a combat prototype, that means working out who the person was in the living world, what their unfinished business was, and what they looked like while alive. Then a larger strike team, with someone from each discipline, hears the pitch of the backstory and abilities. The team gives them "as few visuals as possible", usually just a living-world drawing, and lets them decide how the character will look, sound and move. "That kickoff pitch and backstory is the North Star that we keep referring back to throughout the process."

"I think the best cosmetics do more than simply make a character look different," Bowden says. "They give players another way to express themselves, and ideally they reveal something interesting about the world." Every cosmetic reflects something about who that person was in the living world, an area of the Tower, or "an ecology or culture that has developed over aeons in this afterlife."

The team also decided early that although cosmetics are often designed as cohesive sets, players can mix and match between them. "Arkheron is ultimately about cool combinations of items and cosmetics are no exception," he says. "We've already got some awesome and unanticipated cosmetic combos that our team has put together during our playtests."

Identity, memory and transformation are already central to the world, which he says makes exploring different looks for a character feel natural. "I'll give a funny example just to illustrate that," he says. Someone in the living world may have been a baker, and the team could design a baker-themed Echo. But in the lore, that baker may have spent a thousand years in the Tower, mostly in one of the Builders' areas, say the Archivist's level. "That same Echo may now totally take on the look of the level they inhabit vs. what they do or don't remember from the living world."

Readability sets the limits. "A cosmetic should never leave another player confused about what they're fighting or what's happening on screen," Bowden says. He describes an emote for the Armored Swan skin where you pop angelic wings. "I would have loved to have you fly or float in the air when you use it, but that would be terrible for gameplay and add a lot of player confusion." Size is off the table too, as he says, "I can't have a character skin that is two times larger than the other skins because our hitboxes need to stay consistent for combat and we wouldn't want a player confused for an enemy NPC."

"One of the most important things we keep beating the drum on is that visual quality isn't necessarily about putting more things on screen," Bowden says. "Often, it's about knowing what to leave out. I like to think of polish as an act of conscious removal."

Combat is crowded, and there's a natural temptation to make every character, ability, effect and environment as spectacular as possible. "I think that's a trap that happens when you look at any one of those facets in a vacuum," he says. What guards against it is that the whole team plays every day. "My favourite thing about the culture of the whole Arkheron team is that we all play the game every day. That forces all of us to look at everything in context and as a whole and not as one detail over on your own desktop."

That leads to a set of questions he keeps asking. "What should the player notice first? What's important to gameplay? What can remain atmospheric or understated?" Lighting gives environments mood and personality, but it also has to support character and combat readability. Visual effects should make abilities feel powerful and satisfying while letting players understand what's happening and respond.

On PC, PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S, the goal is simple. "One of our goals has been to make Arkheron feel like Arkheron regardless of where you're playing it." The game was built from the start to feel great on controller as well as mouse and keyboard, which affects performance, readability, responsiveness, and how much information players see.

Platforms have different technical constraints, so the team has to decide where to spend its resources. "I think there's an important difference between preserving every individual visual detail and preserving the artistic intent," he says. The team wants to deliver the atmosphere, character identities, combat clarity, and overall feeling of the world consistently. "And frankly, being disciplined about performance and readability often makes the game better for everyone, regardless of platform. Speaking for myself, the aspect that excites me the most is being able to play with my friends regardless of our hardware of choice."

"I hope their first reaction is curiosity," Bowden says. A video, and especially a screenshot, is likely to give the wrong impression of how the game plays. "You might see that isometric camera and think it's a point-and-click game, or you may see that it is PVP and think it's going to play like a MOBA. It won't." The art, the lore and the gameplay, he says, "are familiar ingredients that are combined in a really original way."

It's a game where you're constantly learning: discovering equipment, trying ability combinations, figuring out how to cooperate with teammates, and outplaying opponents. "There's something incredibly satisfying about the moment when all of that starts to click." The art's job is to make that journey feel exciting and intuitive, with a world that captures the imagination, characters and abilities that make you feel powerful, and visual feedback that explains why you succeeded or failed.

His hope for the first hour: "If a player finishes their first hour thinking, 'I have no idea how good I could get at this, but I really want to find out,' I think we've accomplished something pretty special."

Visit Arkheron and sign up to the playtest. The game enters Early Access on Friday, 27 November, 2026, for PC (Windows), PlayStation 5, and Xbox Series X|S.

#9065. UK government blocks export of 17th-century British landscape painting

English School, A birds-eye view of Llannerch park, Denbighshire, 1662

Department for Digital, Culture, Media & Sport

The UK government has placed an export bar on a 17th-century painting of the Welsh estate Llannerch Park in Denbighshire, northeast Wales, thought to be the earliest known British country-estate landscape painting.

The export ban, which allows time for a UK gallery or institution to acquire the work, will initially expire on 19 February 2027, after which the owners will have 15 business days to consider any offers at the recommended price of £550,000 (plus VAT of £11,000), followed by a second deferral period of four months.

The painting, made around 1662 by an unknown artist, gives a bird’s-eye view of the house and Italian-style gardens at Llannerch Park which “contained a series of marvellous watery innovations: pools, fountains, sculpture, cascades and hydraulic surprises all set off by Baroque architecture, staircases and planting”, says Pippa Shirley, a member of the reviewing committee on the export of works of art and objects of cultural interest which advises the government. The fact that the garden is now lost makes the painting more important, she adds in a statement.

The Llannerch Park garden was created by the landowner Mutton Davies following a tour of France and Italy; according to Sotheby’s, which offered the painting in a sale in 2014 in London, Davies also commissioned the landscape painting in the 1660s, and had remained in the family since. The work failed to sell at the 2014 auction, where it was estimated to sell at £400,000-£600,000. A government spokesperson declined to provide further details regarding the painting's ownership. A slightly smaller version of the painting is housed at the Yale Center for British Art in Connecticut.

“If the painting remains in the UK, researchers will be given the opportunity to explore how people and culture were spreading between Wales, England and the European continent in the seventeenth century. It could also reveal new details about how the artistry of country-estate landscapes developed in Britain,” according to the UK Department for Digital, Media, Culture and Sport.

Offered at Sotheby's London for between £3m and £5m, it is the first painting by the Northern Renaissance master to come to the market in decades

#9063. Programa software tracks everything from product dimensions to material quantities

Studio operations software Programa has redesigned its programme to rethink how interior design studios operate, giving practices more flexibility and freeing up their time.

According to Programa, beautiful interiors are built on “hundreds of decisions”, which take long periods of time to decide upon and update across multiple spreadsheets.

Each decision brings specification details, quantities, pricing and revisions that studios must keep updated as a project develops.

These include minute, precise details such as dimensions, materials, finishes, technical requirements, and component quantities.

Programa‘s redesigned programme keeps a record of each item used in an interior project, from furniture and lighting to hardware and finishes, and optimises their organisation based on how the project runs.

The company explained that increased AI use is making convincing images “easier to generate than ever”, yet clients often run into logistical issues when using this alone.

For example, the AI model doesn’t take into account whether a wardrobe or sofa fits through the door, suits the needs of the people living there, or whether the overall design takes full advantage of a space’s natural light.

With Programa, the designer can smoothly make these judgements using the software’s organisation of specifications, cost, quantities and overall project coordination.

The company explained that if a designer updates a product’s shared specification once, the change appears in the Programa schedules that include it, while quantities can be individually allocated by room.

For Austin Carrier of Californian design studio, Hommeboys Interiors, this is particularly helpful.

“We use schedules for everything from lighting and hardware to plumbing fixtures and furniture, indoor and outdoor,” Carrier explained.

“For furniture, we can break down every room, then the pieces within that room, and give clients several options to reject or accept,” he added.

As a result, the software aims to cut the “gruelling amount of work” updating schedules, preparing presentations, and communicating with suppliers. It also reduces repeated data entry, freeing up time.

The platform is defined as an “alternative to spreadsheets”, which often have to be made from scratch and reformatted for different presentations.

“The issue with the spreadsheet is that it’s like a blank cell,” added Los Angeles-based designer Paul Chan. “You can put anything in there – it doesn’t carry from one project to another.”

“With Programa, I can take a format from one project and move it into the next,” Chan continued. “There’s consistency between each project.”

Specifically, the Programa Schedule function details the items’ code, supplier, finish, dimensions, quantity and price.

It offers a streamlined place to reference drawings, get client approval and work with contractors to meet on-site deadlines.

The company explained that one of its platform’s main benefits is that it can be used from early product decision-making through to final delivery.

Here, the studio manages the specification and controls what is shared, whereas the clients review selections and provide approvals. Collaborators also receive the information relevant to their work.

“Once we get all of the information in there, we can send it out in one email to all of our vendors, and then they are able to get us pricing back very easily,” added Tana Nesbitt-Hayes of Studio 8 Architect.

“If we’re exceeding our budget in one area, we can tailor it back. It’s always up-to-date.”

“We share our Programa Schedules with the millworkers and the engineers,” she added. “They can see the refrigerator we’re going to put in, and they can make the panels to fit.”

Programa offers a free trial for all studios. To learn more, visit its website.
