#9062. A New Museum in Georgia’s Wine Country Shows Another Side of the Country’s Art History

A long journey from Tokyo to the island of Naoshima to see art gave Jemal Inaishvili, a shipping executive and collector, an idea for how he might convince people to make a similar trek within his home country of Georgia in the South Caucasus. Unlike visiting Naoshima, which typically involves a full day of travel, the drive from the capital city of Tbilisi to Kakheti, Georgia’s eastern wine region, is around two hours, three in heavy traffic. “Of course, I cannot copy them,” he told me recently, “but I will do something similar, but based on Georgian art.”

The result is the Kvareli Foundation for Contemporary Art, which opened to the public earlier this month on land Inaishvili bought a decade ago for a small winery. The site now also holds a hotel, a sculpture park, and a red-slatted museum with a rooftop for performances and film screenings by the Tbilisi practice Midamo. This admission-free venue will stage four exhibitions a year, drawing from Inaishvili’s collection of about 1,000 works.

To lead the programming, Inaishvili has hired 28-year-old Nino Sulkhanishvili. “Sometimes one’s experience will be the barrier,” he said of the creative director, who is in her first institutional role. “Together with the foundation, she is also growing.”

In heading up a private museum, Sulkhanishvili sees her role as helping to give Georgian artists the infrastructure to exhibit at home, like Elene Chantladze, whose solo show will open at the Kvareli Foundation in February. Such a setting, Sulkhanishvili said, “is extremely important, especially in your own country. … I feel Georgian artists deserve much more.” Location, too, matters: “contemporary art needs to be decentralized,” she said, noting the foundation’s aim to create an art ecosystem by bringing schoolchildren to visit and training local guides. A residency for both local and international artists will launch next year.

But Georgian art won’t be the foundation’s only focus after the first two years. The collection also includes work by Ukrainian, Turkish, and Armenian artists, which will be shown in the future. In the years to come, Sulkhanishvili hopes to build exchanges with neighboring and post-Soviet countries before looking further afield. “We really want to be a beacon within the region,” she said.

The inaugural exhibition, “Georgian Contemporary Art: Origins and Continuities” (on view through January 15), came together only six months before opening. Instead of just focusing solely on Inaishvili’s collection, Sulkhanishvili proposed a historical survey of the artists who worked outside the Soviet era’s state-sanctioned socialist realism. The show gathers 57 artists from the 1960s to the present, with roughly half the works from his collection and the rest on loan. “Even in the national museums, you don’t see everything together,” Sulkhanishvili said of the artists on view, many of whom are still often “excluded from the [official] narrative” of this moment in Georgian history. This time around, socialist realist artists are intentionally left out.

Irena Popiashvili, the dean of the Visual Arts, Architecture and Design School at Tbilisi’s Free University, said the importance of a show like this could not be understated when state museums often only focus a handful of national artists, like Georgia’s most celebrated painter Niko Pirosmani. “As an educator, it’s important for me, for example, to refer my students [to this show] and for them to be able to see the continuation of the Georgian art history, 20th century throughout and the beginning of the 21st,” she said.

The survey begins with the Thaw that followed Stalin’s death in 1953, when socialist realism remained doctrine but foreign magazines, like ARTnews and Art in America, trickled in. A pioneering figure of Abstract Expressionism in Georgia, Shura Bandzeladze saw a black-and-white reproduction of a Jackson Pollock in Art in America and took it as proof he was “on the right track,” according to Sulkhanishvili.

The risks of deviating from socialist realism were real, though. Ushangi Khumarashvili, a set designer from Kakheti’s largest city, Telavi, clashed with his director and was sent to a psychiatric hospital. On his release, he burned his earlier work and turned to abstraction. In 1974, non-conformist painter and graphic artist Otar Chkhartishvili took part in the unapproved avant-garde Bulldozer Exhibition in Moscow, which the authorities violently broke up. In Levan Chogoshvili’s painting 1924 (ca. 1980s), a dog carries a severed human hand, an image drawn from his grandmother’s account of Bolshevik executions, an episode that official Soviet histories left out. In an officially atheist country, even a return to earlier Western art traditions and the Christian themes they drew on could be equally dangerous. In 1978, Irakli Parjiani began writing out the Gospels by hand and illustrating them in the manner of medieval manuscripts, which Popiashvili described as “a revolutionary act.”

Upstairs, with perestroika in the years before the collapse of the USSR, the mood turns more hopeful. “Even though there was still censorship, even though there was the Soviet Union, there was the sense of optimism,” Sulkhanishvili said, “that something was about to happen, something was about to change.” Artists no longer worked only against the system but began building their own scene, and their canvases began to grow in scale, too. The 10th Floor group, named for its studio at the Tbilisi State Academy of Arts, later moved into a theater workshop large enough for them to realize monumental paintings. Its intellectual leader, artist and art historian Karlo Kacharava, introduced his peers to Western writers: one work here pays tribute to Allen Ginsberg. Keti Kapanadze, whom Sulkhanishvili calls Georgia’s first woman conceptual artist, plays with gender in her “Probable Need” series (1990), for which she drew over photographic self-portraits, representing herself as “Native,” “Mystery,” and “Gentleman.”

By the 1990s, war and chaos in the wake of the collapse of the USSR are answered with bitter humor. Kote Sulaberidze’s video Playing War (1994) restages the 1992–93 war in Abkhazia, a breakaway region under Russian-backed control that Georgia and most of the world regard as occupied Georgian territory, as a children’s game through a tragic yet absurd lens. Nearby, his painted portrait of former Georgian president and Soviet foreign minister Eduard Shevardnadze takes its title, A Face of Caucasian Nationality (1996), from a Russian slur.

The exhibition’s final rooms turn inward, where no common movement or aesthetic prevails, though many of the artists are connected via their drawing on their personal histories. Vajiko Chachkhiani’s 2026 installation one wind after another (2026), for example, comprises recycled Georgian calfskin sewn around everyday objects, like the kind of ice cream sold during in his childhood. A metaphor for a period now gone, only the outer forms of these ice cream boxes remain.

Some artists try to contend with the unease of the recent past. Andro Eradze’s Nightvision, Limited Access (2021) is a short, poetic video of domesticated dogs abandoned during the pandemic and left to run loose, while his digital print Flow State (2025), of a taxidermy monkey in a hat, alludes to humans being locked in. In a sign of Georgian artists’ increasing international visibility, another of Eradze’s videos is now in the collection of the Museum of Modern Art in New York.

The Kvareli Foundation opens at a tense moment in Georgia. A significant portion of Georgia’s art community joined the mass protests in 2023–24 against the “foreign influence” law, which requires NGOs and media groups that receive foreign funding to register as serving foreign interests. (Critics, who call it the “Russian law,” say it mirrors legislation Moscow has used to silence dissent and that it threatens Georgia’s bid to join the EU. The international watchdog group Human Rights Watch warned it would “marginalize and stifle critical voices.”)

Further protests followed the parliamentary elections in October 2024, which some claimed were fraudulent. International watchdogs describe a coordinated crackdown on dissent under the ruling Georgian Dream party, with activists and journalists facing detention, fines, and prosecution, and an ongoing lawsuit before the Constitutional Court that aims to ban five opposition parties, including the United National Movement, founded by former Georgian President Mikheil Saakashvili and of which Inaishvili was a member.

This tense political situation is one many young artists now live abroad, where they also have better opportunities to show their work and sustain themselves as artists. That is partly why Sulkhanishvili did not want to shy away from including political work from the Soviet era with contemporary works that are less explicitly political. Still, she hopes visitors will see Georgia as a country still in flux. “I will be happy here if someone comes in and can see the line, how things were changing,” she said.

On the current state of the country, Sulkhanishvili strikes a different tone to the foundation’s founder; Inaishvili’s tenure as deputy chair of parliament from 2004 to 2008 is central to Georgian Dream’s ongoing lawsuit, which alleges that Saakashvili’s government is the root of the opposition parties’ wrongdoing that the ruling party hopes to root out. Inaishvili insists that people “don’t know me as a politician.”

During the opening, he reported no pressure from the government to show a certain kind of art or mount exhibitions from a specific perspective. “Every government likes when this kind of project is happening,” he said, particularly when it is privately funded. He called the overall situation “quite okay” and said artists have always been in opposition.

Sulkhanishvili is warier of the political realities of state interference, saying that while overt censorship may no longer be mandated, there is still a chilling effect that impacts the kind of art that can be made and shown in Georgia. As such, she does not plan to collaborate with state museums in order to protect the foundation’s independence. That independence rests largely on Inaishvili’s money; he has already sunk more than €25 million ($27.4 million) into the project, though funding for its continuation will be partly helped by the hotel income.

“We’re not attacking anyone. We’re just not asking anything from them,” Sulkhanishvili said, adding, “We’re not neutral in any way.” The inaugural group show’s aim to change the story of what Georgian contemporary art has been, she said, “is our statement.”

#9060. Fatbergs, pigeons and Pankhurst: rebranded London Museum opens new £437m home

The London sign mounted on a former awning structure that bridges between the former General Market and Market Annexe at Smithfield Market © Hufton + Crow

The new London Museum based at the historic Smithfield Market in Farringdon—one of the biggest museum developments in the UK capital in recent years—will open to the public this week with exhibits including a “fatberg” from the sewers, the Suffragette Emmeline Pankhurst’s hunger strike medal and Roman writing tablets.

Emmeline Pankhurst’s hunger strike medal © London Museum

Based at London Wall near the Barbican Centre until it closed in December 2022, the institution was previously called the Museum of London. The new complex, one of Europe’s largest cultural infrastructure projects, is designed by Stanton Williams and Asif Khan in partnership with the conservation architects Julian Harrap.

The museum caused a stir in 2024 when it unveiled a rebrand centred around the image of a defecating pigeon. Sharon Ament, the museum director, tells The Art Newspaper: “It’s not often a museum brand gets into the news. I think that’s because people saw, in our pigeon, the city and their experience: a place full of contrasts. It’s beautiful, it’s fun, it’s also a bit scruffy! I don’t think there’s a better representation of us than a pigeon.”

The first phase of the London Museum will open in a Victorian part of the Smithfield Market © Secchi Smith

The new museum site will open in two phases: the formerly derelict Victorian General Market dating from the 1880s, home to the permanent galleries, will open on 28 November, while the 1960s Poultry Market, which houses a learning centre, temporary exhibition spaces and on-site interactive collection store, will launch in 2028.

“We are using time as an organising principle, so our major spaces all behave differently with their own emphasis, objects and vibe,” says Ament. The General Market houses the Past Time and Our Time sections, plus Night Time. Past Time spans 2,000 years, telling the story of London via landmark events like the Great Fire in 1666 and the 2012 Olympics.

A chunk of the Whitechapel Fatberg © London Museum

“Stars of the collection” like the Cheapside Hoard of Elizabethan and Jacobean jewels; the medal given to Pankhurst to commemorate her 1912 hunger strike; and a sample of the fatberg—a 250-metre long mass of oil and wet wipes—will also feature in Past Time.

“We have two significant but very contrasting buildings in the Victorian General Market and the listed 1960s Poultry Market, representing different moments in London’s history. We think about them as two of the biggest objects in our collection and they lend themselves to different experiences,” says Ament.

Our Time in the Linbury Hall is a social hub at the heart of London Museum, set across the former trading floor of the General Market. Around its perimeter, a restaurant, shop and show space for families and schools sits alongside 13 large installations exploring the ways Londoners have come together © Hufton + Crow

Asked if the museum is just for Londoners, she says that the city’s residents will discover new stories from the city’s vast history, and be part of telling its story today, while for international visitors, “this is a great first place to start their immersion in London”. The museum has an ambitious visitor figure target of over two million annually.

There are 18 people in the curatorial team but the museum is also supported by an academic advisory panel and “some 100,000 people from London and beyond” who have helped shaped the museum. These include various focus groups, community and school groups, and advisory panels such as the museum’s Access Panel and Family Panel

View into part of London Museum’s "London Tastes" display, exploring the changing appetites of a global food city © Hufton + Crow

The cost of the new museum has risen to £437m in total (the budget was set at £337m in 2019). The Greater London Authority, under mayor Sadiq Khan, has given £95m, while the City of London Corporation is contributing £222m. A range of private foundations and sponsors including Bloomberg Philanthropies, the Goldsmiths’ Foundation, the Linbury Trust and the National Lottery Heritage Fund are also backing the project.

As for running costs, statutory funding comes from the City of London Corporation and the Mayor of London, Ament says.

“We also want to find ways to stand on our own feet more,” she says. “That means support from commercial partnerships and activities, like retail, ticket sales, our ‘fan club’ [the museum’s membership] and venue hire. We’re also leasing spaces, known as the museum ‘Houses’, that sit around the perimeter of the General Market, so now we are landlords as well.” She says the sites are sustainable through the use of solar panels and smart technology.

The Stratford-based museum, opening this month, aims to build on the success of V&A East Storehouse, which has attracted 500,000 visitors since it opened in May last year

The revamped museum, which focuses on the history of the UK capital, will open to the public on 28 November 2026

Galleries on lockdown connect online during coronavirus pandemic using #CollectionsUnited

The proposals include growing commercial opportunities, using technologies to support itineraries and for the museum to be informative about its wider history

Production Type refused to let this Parisian classic die.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Paris-based foundry Production Type has revived the classic French typeface Vendôme, restoring it to its former glory. Once tainted by poor handwritten recreations and clunky scans, the font eventually lost its lustre, but with patience and craft, Production Type has revitalised this classic for the better.

In its early days, Vendôme was one of the best serif fonts – a celebration of France's post-WWII creative boom. Making a playful, contemporary debut, the new Vendôme Nouveau is a love letter to French heritage, with a elegant, modern refinement.

Vendôme first made its debut back in 1950, drawn by sculptor and set designer François Ganeau, with meticulous art direction from Roger Excoffon. Defined by its "leaning stems, wavering strokes, plunging Vs, and abruptly sharp serifs," the typeface became an icon of design, featuring on ads, book jackets, record sleeves, and film posters.

But the legendary font soon began to suffer from its own success, being recreated by sign painters and shopkeepers who wanted a slice of its fame. With the rise of phototypesetting, the font was endlessly copied, and by the 90s, the iconic typeface had countless iterations with varying degrees of quality and style.

Refusing to let the icon die, the Production Type team (and type historian PhDs) set about restoring the font to its former glory. A labour of love, the process took over 20 years of meticulous redrawing, using an array of archival paper proofs and filling the gaps of missing weights from scratch.

The font made an unconventional and wonderfully contemporary debut on the NYC subway, where commuters were snapped reading fake typographic self-help books like “How to Raise a Sans Serif in an All-Serif Family”.

Discover more about the project or take a look at the most iconic typefaces ever made.

#9058. Frieze Los Angeles Lines Up 102 Exhibitors for 2027 Edition

Frieze Los Angeles has named the 102 exhibitors that will participate in its upcoming 2027 edition, scheduled to run February 25–28 at the Santa Monica Airport.

The line-up includes several returning blue-chip galleries like Gagosian, Hauser & Wirth, Pace Gallery, David Zwirner, White Cube, Lisson, Gladstone, Sprüth Magers, and Thaddaeus Ropac. Galleries returning to the fair after an absence include Regen Projects, Luis De Jesus Los Angeles, Mariane Ibrahim, and Petzel.

Though several LA-based galleries and LA outposts for larger galleries have closed in the past year and a half, Frieze LA will feature 38 exhibitors with spaces in the City of Angels. They include Commonwealth and Council, Vielmetter, Marc Selwyn Fine Art, Charlie James, Night Gallery, Parker Gallery, Roberts Projects, and Make Room, which has been promoted to the main Galleries section. Related Articles This LA Exhibition of Julia Stoschek's Video Art Collection Is the City's Hottest Ticket  Nor'easter Causes Travel Delays for New York Dealers Heading to Frieze Los Angeles

“Los Angeles has many centers, each with its own history and communities, and you feel that in the work artists make here: the personal histories they draw on and the questions they’re asking about belonging and who public space is for,” Frieze Americas director Christine Messineo said in a statement. “For the city’s galleries, this is their hometown fair, a moment for the whole LA art world to show the work being made now, by artists across generations. What I love is that visitors from around the world get to experience this work right where it comes from.”

The fair will feature 22 first-time exhibitors, with 10 of them coming from the Focus section, for emerging galleries, which will be organized by Hammer curator Erin Christovale. They consist of four LA galleries, including Rajiv Menon Contemporary and House of Seiko, and six New York galleries, including Entrance, King’s Leap, and Gladwell Projects. Galleries making their debut in the main section include Gallery Wendi Norris, G Gallery, and Yehudi Hollander-Pappi.

At the fair’s entrance, visitors will be met with LA-based artist rafa esparza’s Queercancha, which will take the form of two painted adobe panels supported by a steel armature showing a scene of queer Latinxs cruising in a lowrider in the 1990s. The commission comes shortly after Hauser & Wirth announced its representation of esparza earlier this month. Additionally, his painting WeDGAF (2026) will be the main marketing image for the 2027 fair, appearing on billboards and digital screens in partnership with Orange Barrel Media, the company founded by ARTnews Top 200 Collector Pete Scantland.

“Every city brings something distinct to our network,” Frieze executive director of fairs Kristell Chadé said in a statement. “In Los Angeles, it’s how closely the visual arts sit alongside the city’s other creative industries. The fair is an opportunity for galleries and artists to connect with a collecting community that reaches into film, music, design and technology.”

#9057. Seaweed earplug among grant-winning Design Museum prototypes

A single-use earplug crafted from seaweed, two plant-based insulation materials and a homegrown timber kit-of-parts for low-rise buildings are among the projects that have been awarded Design Museum grants.

UK-based studios Searo Labs, WeCanMake, Local Works Studio and SY Ecofit have been granted a share of £280,000 from the Design Museum for their “cutting-edge” environmental prototypes.

Described as the “world’s first seaweed-based single-use earplug”, SearoSoft by Cambridge-based Searo Labs is a fully biodegradable and renewable alternative to single-use earplugs.

According to SearoSoft, the soft, mouldable earplugs are made without microplastics or chemicals and designed to hydrate the ear canal, unlike plastic-based products, which can be drying.

Once discarded, they are biodegradable in water or soil after 30 days. As seaweed is a regenerative crop, SearoSoft explained that there is no need for land, freshwater or fertilisers, making the process simple and more sustainable.

Among the other prototypes is a building material project by Sussex-based Local Works Studio. The initiative, named Ferment, will repurpose agricultural waste into an insulating material fit for retrofitting buildings.

Local Works Studio aims to develop an accessible product for farms via what it calls a “harvest-to-house system”, where farmers can produce the insulation themselves using their existing infrastructure, skills and machinery.

Bristol-based studio WeCanMake’s winning prototype, Neighbourhood Factory Futures, is a homegrown timber kit-of-parts system designed to be used for constructing low-rise apartment buildings.

With the Design Museum’s grant, the studio plans to create a neighbourhood factory model, allowing local communities to build and maintain their own homes.

WeCanMake explained it created the system as part of a wider movement aiming to make the UK a “nation of growers, producers and makers” while using reusable materials that store, rather than emit, carbon.

Prototyping PhytoFloc by social enterprise SY Ecofit in collaboration with Phyona and Studio Bio is a zero-waste project that, similarly to Local Works Studio, aims to develop plant-based insulation for building construction.

The project uses biowaste created as a byproduct of phytomining, where former industrial land is rejuvenated by plants that extract pollutants from the soil.

The project intends to recognise the value of post-industrial soils while creating a locally made, low-carbon material.

The grants are part of the Design Museum’s Future Observatory program, which is run in partnership with the Arts and Humanities Research Council. The winning projects were amongst 140 prototypes that were submitted to the scheme.

The museum explained that at a time when supply chains are under pressure, the Future Observatory aims to support designers’ practical research to drive the green transition.

“The climate crisis demands rapid change, and we believe that design is critically important if we are to meet that challenge,” said Design Museum director Tim Marlow.

“The presence of Future Observatory allows us an extraordinary opportunity to get involved with practitioners and problem-solvers and have a direct impact on the development of new technologies at the frontier of current design thinking.”

The four projects will be funded from November 2026 until July 2027. Afterwards, the prototypes will be tested and begin the commercialisation process.

Picture this: you're standing at the gate for your Boston weekend trip, and the person next to you just swiped their credit card for $280 to book the exact same seat you're sitting in — a seat that cost you 7,500 Avios and maybe $5.60 in taxes. That's the British Airways Avios short-haul sweet spot in action, and once you see it, you can never unsee it. This is the redemption the ChooseFI community quietly uses to stretch their points further than almost any other domestic award. While everyone else is chasing first-class international awards (which are spectacular, don't get us wrong), this sweet spot lets you turn a modest points balance into a steady stream of nearly free regional flights — year-round, on American Airlines metal, with zero fuel surcharges. Here's the math that makes it click: A last-minute nonstop flight from New York (JFK/LGA) to Boston Logan or Los Angeles (LAX) to San Francisco typically runs anywhere from $150 to $300 in cash. You're paying that for roughly a one-hour flight — the kind of trip where by the time the flight attendant hands you a drink, you're already starting your descent. British Airways prices that same flight at a flat **7,500 Avios**. At a $200 cash fare, that's **2.67 cents per point (CPP)** — well above the standard valuation most programs offer for domestic economy. At a $300 last-minute fare, you're looking at **4 cents per point**, which is exceptional for any award program, let alone a simple domestic booking. The pricing inefficiency is hiding in plain sight: British Airways uses a **distance-based award chart**, which means short flights cost proportionally fewer points. The U.S. domestic short-haul zone (under 650 miles) sits at 7,500 Avios one-way — a price that hasn't ballooned with inflation the way cash fares have. Every time airfare spikes for a holiday weekend or a last-minute booking, your Avios redemption looks better and better. For the FI-minded traveler, this redemption is pure arbitrage: you're converting transferable points that cost you perhaps 1–1.5 cents each to earn into travel worth 2–4 cents each in real-world value. That's a 2–4x return, consistently, on routes you'd likely be flying anyway.

The magic here lives inside British Airways' distance-based award chart — and understanding why it's structured this way is the 'aha moment' that turns a confusing loyalty program into a tool you actually want to use.

Most U.S. airline programs (Delta, United, American) have largely abandoned distance-based pricing in favor of dynamic or zone-based awards that tend to price popular routes higher. British Airways never fully made that switch for partner awards. Their Avios chart still prices flights primarily by the number of miles flown between origin and destination. A flight under 650 miles costs 7,500 Avios one-way in economy — full stop. It doesn't matter if it's a Tuesday in February or the Sunday after Thanksgiving. The chart price holds.

The Partner Piece: Why You're Booking AA, Not BA

Here's the critical nuance that trips up new users: British Airways charges notoriously high fuel surcharges on its own operated flights. We're talking $300–800+ in carrier-imposed fees on top of the Avios. That would completely wipe out the value of this redemption. But when you book American Airlines-operated flights through British Airways Avios, those surcharges disappear entirely. AA does not pass fuel surcharges to partner award bookings. Your out-of-pocket cost is typically just the government taxes — often $5–15 each way.

This is the non-negotiable rule: always book AA metal through British Airways Avios, not BA-operated flights.

Avios are one of the most accessible award currencies in the ecosystem. You can transfer from four major transferable points programs at a 1:1 ratio:

Marriott Bonvoy® also transfers to Avios at a 3:1 ratio (3 Marriott points = 1 Avios), and Marriott throws in a 5,000 Avios bonus for every 60,000 Marriott points transferred. That's a less efficient path for this redemption, but worth knowing.

The 355-day booking window means you can transfer and book nearly a full year in advance — critical for holiday travel or high-demand routes.

British Airways allows open-jaw routing on Avios awards. That means you could theoretically fly into one city and out of a nearby city without paying for two separate awards — useful if you're exploring a region and want flexibility. For short domestic hops, this opens up creative itinerary options that pure point-to-point programs don't allow.

Before you touch your Avios balance, go to aa.com and run a standard flight search for your route. When the results load, look specifically for flights labeled 'Web Special' or filter by lowest MileSAAver awards. You're searching for American's own award inventory — the same inventory British Airways can see and book. If AA shows saver-level availability (the lowest award tier), British Airways will almost certainly be able to book it too.

This step saves you frustration. Don't transfer points until you've confirmed the flight you want is bookable at the saver level.

Double-check that your route qualifies for the 7,500 Avios tier by confirming it's under 650 miles. NYC to Boston is about 187 miles. LAX to SFO is about 337 miles. Both qualify easily. A quick Google search — '[City A] to [City B] flight distance miles' — gives you the straight-line distance. When in doubt, routes you'd describe as 'short regional hops' within the same metro corridor will almost always qualify.

Go to britishairways.com, log into (or create) your Executive Club account, and run an Avios award search for the same route and dates. You should see the American Airlines flight(s) appear at 7,500 Avios + a small tax amount — typically $5–$15. If the flight shows up here, you're ready to book.

Once you've confirmed availability, it's time to transfer. Here's what to do based on your points currency:

Important: Only transfer what you need. Points transferred to British Airways cannot be moved back.

Return to BA's award search (refresh if needed), select your American Airlines flight, and complete the booking. You'll pay the Avios from your balance plus the small tax amount with a credit card. You'll receive an American Airlines confirmation number, which you can use at aa.com to manage your reservation, select seats, and add TSA PreCheck or Known Traveler Numbers.

If your ideal date shows no saver inventory, try:

Let's make this concrete. It's mid-October and you want to visit a college friend in Boston for the weekend — flying out of New York's JFK on a Friday evening, returning Sunday afternoon.

You pull up Google Flights. Friday evening nonstops from JFK to BOS? The cheapest is $189. The convenient 6:30 PM departure on American Airlines is $229. Sunday afternoon return is another $199. Round-trip cash cost: $428.

You check aa.com and confirm both flights show saver-level award availability. You open British Airways' site and find:

You transfer 15,000 Chase Ultimate Rewards points to British Airways — it arrives instantly. You book both flights through BA, receive your AA confirmation numbers, and log into aa.com to select your seats.

If those flights had crept up to $300 each (not unusual around Columbus Day weekend), you'd be looking at 4 cents per point — outstanding for a domestic economy booking.

You're on a standard American Airlines narrow-body — likely a Boeing 737 or Airbus A319. It's economy, which for a 45-minute flight is entirely appropriate. You'll get a beverage service, overhead bin space, and you land at the same gate, use the same terminal, and have the same on-time performance as any other passenger on that plane. The difference is that they paid $229 and you paid $5.60 plus some points that cost you roughly $150 to earn through everyday spending.

That's the FI mindset applied to travel: same experience, radically different cost.

Do This: Book Up to 355 Days Out for Holiday Travel BA's booking window opens 355 days in advance, and American releases its best saver space early. If you're targeting Thanksgiving weekend, Christmas, or a peak summer Friday, set a calendar reminder to search at the 355-day mark. Award seats on popular routes at peak times go fast.

Do This: Use the Open-Jaw Rule Creatively BA allows open-jaw routing on Avios awards. If you're flying into NYC but want to return from a different airport — say JFK inbound and EWR outbound — you may be able to structure this as a single open-jaw award rather than two separate bookings. Worth exploring for multi-city weekend trips.

Avoid This: Booking BA-Operated Flights with This Strategy This cannot be overstated — BA's own flights carry $300–800+ in carrier-imposed surcharges. If you accidentally book a British Airways codeshare or BA-metal flight instead of an American Airlines-operated flight, you'll owe hundreds in fees. Always verify the operating carrier before confirming. Look for 'Operated by American Airlines' in the booking details.

Avoid This: Transferring Points Before Confirming Availability Points transferred to British Airways are one-way and permanent. Never transfer until you have eyes on the specific flight, date, and saver availability you want. The 30-second search on BA's site before transferring is non-negotiable.

Do This: Keep Your Account Active Avios expire after 36 months of account inactivity. If you accumulate Avios for a future trip, make sure to earn or redeem at least a small amount every three years. Even a small shopping portal purchase through the BA Executive Club keeps your balance alive.

Do This: Stack with Other Short Hops Think about recurring trips in your life — quarterly visits to family, annual conferences, weekend trips to a nearby city. This sweet spot isn't just for one redemption; it's a repeatable system. A modest Avios balance of 30,000–45,000 points could cover three to six regional roundtrips per year.

Why distance-based pricing changes the domestic flying equation

Most U.S. airline loyalty programs use region-based or dynamic pricing for award flights, charging the same number of miles whether you fly 200 miles or 2,000. British Airways uses distance-based pricing instead, which means shorter flights cost dramatically fewer Avios. Since BA is a Oneworld partner with American Airlines, you can use Avios to book AA-operated nonstop domestic flights. The result: a flight that AA might price at 12,500-25,000 miles can be booked for just 7,500 Avios through BA. This is one of the most reliable and repeatable sweet spots in travel rewards.

Sign up for a free BA Executive Club account at ba.com. This is where your Avios balance lives and where you will search and book award flights on American Airlines.

Transfer Chase Ultimate Rewards, Amex Membership Rewards, Capital One Miles, or Citi ThankYou Points to your BA Executive Club account. Transfers are typically instant. Only transfer what you need for a specific booking.

On the BA website, search for your route using the "Book with Avios" option. Look for American Airlines-operated nonstop flights. Filter results to find flights coded as AA with available Avios seats.

Confirm the flight is pricing at 7,500 Avios (under 1,151 miles) or 10,000 Avios (1,151-2,000 miles). Check that taxes and fees are the expected $5.60. If prices seem high, try different dates or check that you selected a nonstop flight.

Book the flight and add your AAdvantage number to the reservation so you receive any applicable elite benefits. You will receive a confirmation from British Airways, and the ticket will also appear in your AA account.

Yes. British Airways and American Airlines are both Oneworld alliance members, so you can use BA Avios to book award seats on AA-operated flights. You book directly through the British Airways website (ba.com) and search for AA flight numbers.

Flights under 1,151 miles cost 7,500 Avios each way in economy. Flights between 1,151-2,000 miles cost 10,000 Avios. Flights between 2,001-3,000 miles cost 12,500 Avios. The value proposition is strongest on the shortest flights where the Avios cost is lowest.

Not on domestic American Airlines flights. The typical fee is just $5.60 each way. High fuel surcharges only apply when booking British Airways-operated long-haul flights, not when using Avios on partner airlines like AA domestically.

Chase Ultimate Rewards, Amex Membership Rewards, Capital One Miles, and Citi ThankYou Points all transfer to British Airways Avios. Transfer ratios are 1:1 from Chase, Amex, and Capital One. Transfers are typically instant or within 24 hours.

This sweet spot was practically designed for the ChooseFI beginner — someone who has their first transferable points card (a Chase Sapphire Preferred, an Amex Gold, or a Bilt card) and wants to make a real, tangible redemption without navigating complex routing rules or praying for elusive premium cabin availability.

Minimum to get started: You need at least 7,500 Avios (or transferable points to convert) for a one-way. For a round-trip, 15,000. Most sign-up bonuses — even modest ones — cover multiple round-trips with this sweet spot.

Who this is NOT for: If you're flying coast-to-coast (NYC to LAX is over 2,400 miles — a different, higher Avios tier), this specific pricing won't apply. This sweet spot is purpose-built for short hops under 650 miles. It's also not the move if you already have AA elite status and can snag cheap upgrades — but for the rest of us, it's perfect.

This redemption earns a **5/5 for beginner friendliness** — and that rating is fully deserved. Let's be specific about why. The hardest part of most award bookings is finding available seats and navigating confusing partner systems. This one simplifies both: you're searching a major U.S. airline's (AA) domestic saver inventory, which is widely available on popular short-haul routes year-round. You're not hunting for a specific aircraft with lie-flat seats or hoping a single partner releases one business class seat. Domestic economy saver space is genuinely accessible. The booking process itself is two websites: aa.com to check availability, britishairways.com to book. Neither requires a phone call, neither has complicated routing rules for simple one-way or round-trip domestic bookings, and the transfer from Chase or Amex is instant. **The three things to get right:** 1. **Confirm saver availability on AA before transferring** — This habit protects you from the only real risk (irreversible point transfers). 2. **Verify the operating carrier is American Airlines, not British Airways** — One glance at 'Operated by' in the booking details handles this. 3. **Keep your BA Executive Club account active** — Set a reminder to log in or earn at least once every 36 months so your Avios don't expire. That's genuinely the whole checklist. If you've never booked an award flight before, this is the redemption to start with. You'll build the muscle memory — search, confirm, transfer, book — in about 20 minutes, and you'll have a nearly free flight to show for it. Welcome to travel rewards.

This sweet spot was last verified over 90 days ago. Award availability and pricing may have changed — verify current rates before booking.

Using British Airways Avios for short domestic nonstop flights on American Airlines is one of the most practical and repeatable sweet spots in travel rewards. At just 7,500 Avios each way with $5.60 in fees, it dramatically undercuts what AA charges through its own program. With four major transfer partners feeding BA Avios, this sweet spot is accessible from virtually any points-earning strategy. Whether you are booking a quick NYC-Chicago hop or an LA-San Francisco shuttle, BA Avios should be your first look for short-haul domestic flights.

#9055. Waugh Thistleton Architects set to transform derelict bathing pavilion into Tracey Emin-backed studios and sauna

Images courtesy of Waugh Thistleton Architects

UK studio Waugh Thistleton Architects is set to transform the Edwardian Westbrook Pavilion in Margate, UK, into an arts centre for British artist Tracey Emin with a cafe, public sauna and changing rooms.

“The project will bring a much-loved seafront building back into use, combining its original purpose with new spaces for art, culture and the local community,” said Waugh Thistleton Architects.

The studio recently won planning permission from the local council to convert the abandoned building, which Emin purchased in 2023, into a facility run by the Tracey Emin Foundation.

The project aims to return the building to its former use as a changing room for swimmers and as a tea room, when it originally opened in 1914.

“Originally opened in 1914, the building provided public changing facilities for sea-bathing and a tea room,” said the studio.

“Following storm damage in the Great North Sea Storm of 1953, subsequent alterations detracted from its original Edwardian character,” it continued.

“The renovated pavilion will accommodate artist studios, an art gallery, clubroom, cafe, sea-bathing changing facilities, a new sauna and refurbished public toilets, restoring its original role as a place for bathing and socialising by the sea.”

Along with making the pavilion a building used by the public again, the studio aims to return the building’s core to its Edwardian look by removing later additions. It will also add glazed facades to the wings on either side of the central pavilion.

The building will be topped by a rooftop terrace, while a public toilet on the site will be renovated.

“The design draws on the proportions and character of the original building, removing later additions and reinstating lost features such as the historic belvederes which top the central tower structures,” said the studio.

“The beachfront facade will see a new glazing system and colonnade to each of the building’s wings, with a new sheltered archway forming a new seating terrace at the building’s heart,” it continued.

“The design seeks to reference the original architecture while providing contemporary needs of a public building. Where original features are references, these are distinguishable architecturally.”

Emin is one of the UK’s best-known living artists. We recently produced a video of a landmark exhibition of her work at Tate Modern.

Recent projects by Waugh Thistleton Architects include plans for the “tallest mass timber office building in the US”.

#9054. MacBook Pro 16 (2026, M5 Pro, PROLED XDR) review: the touchscreen Mac is here at last

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Discover design software, tools and creative resources.

Packed with digital art tutorials, inspiration and expert advice from ImagineFX.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A touchscreen MacBook has been on the wishlist of many Mac users (and media commentators) for years, and now it’s finally here. While Apple hasn’t gone all the way and produced a 2-in-1 MacBook with a stylus, there are some applications for the touchscreen tech in creative apps, and the switch to OLED means there's incredible brightness on offer. The big drawback is that it’s even more expensive, especially as it only comes on top-end machines, but one day every MacBook might be like this.

Force Touch trackpad not immediately intuitive

Why you can trust Creative Bloq Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.

There's a lot of ‘pro’ in this laptop. It’s a MacBook Pro. It has an M5 Pro CPU inside it. And it has Apple’s new PROLED XDR screen, which is a touchscreen OLED to everyone else. Is there any way that more pro-ness could have been squeezed in? Perhaps one of the Radeon Pro GPUs that graced the ‘Darth Vader’s dustbin’ generation of the Mac Pro?

That aside, we might be looking at the future of the MacBook line. While for now the new screen is only available on a few top-end models, the benefits it brings - not only improved brightness but a thinner and lighter chassis - are likely to trickle down through the range.

The MacBook Pro remains pro-fessional, has a powerful pro-cessor, and Apple’s hardware pro-wess means we shouldn’t get any pro-blems from the PROLED display. Let’s see. It could be heading to the top of our best laptop for animation guide.

3x Thunderbolt 5, 1x HDMI 2.1, 3.5mm audio

• Slightly slimmer than before• Not a 2-in-1

First things first, the PROLED screen makes the 16in MacBook Pro a little slimmer and lighter. It’s also a stunner in terms of colour and brightness, but Apple is so late to this party it’s a little hard to get overexcited. We’ve had OLED touchscreens on Windows PCs since at least 2016 and Lenovo’s Yoga 14, and while the display tech is magnificent it does mean you end up with fingermarks all over your screen, especially if you’re using it after lunch.

Then there's the debate about what touchscreen laptops are actually for. In 2-in-1 designs you can bend the screen back and whip out a stylus for some sketching, but in a traditional laptop you’re more likely to use it for zooming and scrolling. Apple’s announcement event for the laptop showed someone using the touchscreen to play piano keys directly on its screen, and while this somehow seems unlikely, as surely your hands will be in entirely the wrong position, it can also be used to click and drag files, audio tracks, and to do a little precision brushwork with your fingertip if you need to. Happily, it’s optional, and the MacBook trackpad is as good as ever. The touchscreen supports most trackpad gestures, if you’re the sort to let their fingers dance, and as ever you can pay extra for the Nanotexture coating that cuts reflections.

Elsewhere, you get the usual MacBook Pro build. They’re really well made, and this one’s no exception. The switch to OLED has allowed for a millimetre to be shaved off the laptop’s thickness, and a few hundred grams to be shed from its weight. The weight reduction is the more noticeable of the two, making Apple’s largest laptop a touch more portable. By far the most important thing, however, is that the Apple logo on the MacBook’s lid once again lights up when the laptop is in use, and it’s the right way up.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

• Thunderbolt 5• Excellent colour reproduction

There are three Thunderbolt 5 ports on the MacBook Pro 16, all of which are compatible with USB4 peripherals, and as there's a full-size HDMI 2.1 port and a MagSafe 3 for charging, you won’t have to bog them down connecting to monitors and chargers. This opens them up for use with external SSDs, and given the extra cost of upgrading the storage in a modern Mac when you order, one of those will probably be on your shopping list.

The screen is the big new feature for this 2026 release of the MacBook Pro 16, and this new OLED is an absolute beauty. It’s a ‘tandem’ OLED, which stacks two light-emitting layers on top of one another for a brightness boost, and it shows: Apple promises up to 2,000 nits of brightness if you feed it HDR content, a figure that rivals even its immensely bright Studio Display XDR. Colour is excellent too though you’ll need to manually activate the PROLED XDR P3 + AdobeRGB colour profile in the Settings app to get the most out of it. Do this, and you can expect 93% of Adobe RGB and 94% of DCI-P3 alongside 100% of sRGB.

Apple has also fiddled with the MacBook Pro’s hinge for a better touchscreen experience. Push too hard and you can find a laptop’s screen leaning away from you, but the hinge on the PROLED is noticeably stiffer than that on a non-touch MacBook. It’s also incredibly smooth, almost like there's some sort of hydraulic aspect to it, as it moves up and down.

On the front you’ll find Apple’s usual keyboard, which is pretty good, and a Force Touch trackpad that can take a bit of getting used to, especially if you’re used to holding the pad in to drag files about. This can trigger a deeper click that brings up file information, which is less useful than you might think, but it doesn’t take long to get the hang of, and you can change what it does in the settings.

We test every one of our laptops using the same benchmarking software suite to give you a thorough overview of its suitability for creatives of all disciplines and levels. This includes:

• Geekbench: Tests the CPU for single-core and multi-core power, and the GPU for the system's potential for gaming, image processing, or video editing. Geekbench AI tests the CPU and GPU on a variety of AI-powered and AI-boosted tasks.• Cinebench: Tests the CPU and GPU's ability to run Cinema 4D and Redshift.• UL Procyon: Uses UL Solutions' Procyon software suite to test the system's ability for AI image generation in Stable Diffusion, its Microsoft Office performance and its battery life in a looping video test.• Topaz Video AI: We use Topaz Video AI to test the system's ability to upscale video and convert video to slow-motion.• PugetBench for Creators: We use the PugetBench for Creators benchmarking suite to test the system's ability to run several key tasks in Photoshop and Adobe Premiere Pro, as well as its performance when encoding/transcoding video.• ON1 Resize AI: Tests the system's ability to resize 5 photos to 200% in a batch process. We take the total time taken to resize the images and divide by 5.

• Very fast CPU• GPU can't beat descrete chips

The PROLED MacBook is a premium product, and so comes with a choice of premium processors (and a premium price, but more on that later). It can be fitted with an M5 Pro, which is what we’ve got here, or an M5 Max that piles on the processing cores. There's no option for anything else, so you won’t be picking one up with a vanilla M5 in it. The M5 Pro and Max both use Apple’s Fusion Architecture to weld CPU dies together into one mega-chip, and the core counts make it look very much like the Pro is two normal M5s stuck together, with two cores disabled. It’s split into six Super cores and 12 Performance cores - the old Efficient cores are missing from this generation - and it can turbo up to 4.6 GHz.

Apple’s claim that the M5 offers the fastest single-core performance out there remains unbeaten in our tests. In the Geekbench 6 single-core test, the M5 Pro comes within a hair’s breadth of the M5 Max in a Mac Studio, a remarkable feat for a laptop. The Studio pulls ahead a bit in the multi-core test due to having more cores, but the Pro is right up there, actually beating the M5 Max from when we tested it in a MacBook Pro and leaving the M4 Pro behind.

The fastest non-Apple single-core result in our tests, the Asus Zenbook A16 powered by a Qualcomm Snapdragon X2 Elite, now rests in tenth place in the Geekbench charts, and you have to go to 13th place before you find an X86 CPU, which is in a desktop gaming PC. Apple is completely dominant in this arena at the moment, and it’s only when you switch to the GPU test results that the gaming PCs rise to the top and the Apple chips get some real competition.

In real-world applications, the M5 Pro isn’t as fast at doing tasks such as denoising raw files in Adobe Camera Raw as an Nvidia GPU, but it’s way faster than trying to do it using the integrated graphics on most Intel or AMD chips.

The battery life of all the M5 generation MacBooks has been exceptional, but the OLED screen has tipped the 16in Pro over the edge into a machine that can be relied on for two whole days of use. Testing how long it could play a video until exhausted took a lot longer than on most other laptops, with a final figure in excess of 21 hours. Push it really hard and that will come down, of course, but it’s a remarkable achievement nonetheless.

This is the thing that’s going to keep these first touchscreen Macs out of the hands of many creatives. The 16in model we’ve got here starts at £3,399 for one with 24GB of RAM and 1TB of storage, and just climbs and climbs as you add more stuff to it. You want 64GB of RAM and 4TB of storage? You can have it, but it’ll cost you £5,899 and you can go higher than that if you switch to the M5 Max. The touchscreen is a premium feature, and the same laptop with the old display starts from £2,999. The old M5 model no longer seems to be available, probably to make way for an M6, which is already there on the 14in version.

The fact this laptop even exists means Apple thinks there's a market for it, and if you’re a touchscreen laptop lover it may be the machine you’ve been dreaming of. There's no denying the expense, however, which means you’re really going to have to love it to consider it over other, better-value, choices.

Excellent CPU performance, GPU can't fight Nvidia.

Closer in performance to the MacBook Pro than to the MacBook Neo, the M5 edition of the MacBook Air is the bargain in Apple's range.

The frist generation of Nvidia's RTX Spark hardware looks promising for creatives. This 14-incher from Asus is powerful, well built, beautifully thin and light, and will last all day on a charge.

A mighty gaming laptop with a powerful GPU can make a good buy for a video editor or designer who likes to work on complex documents. This one from HP is slightly more subtly designed than many, and though its battery life is short it can surely speed up your workflows.

Ian Evenden has been a journalist for over 20 years, starting in the days of QuarkXpress 4 and Photoshop 5. He now mainly works in Creative Cloud and Google Docs, but can always find a use for a powerful laptop or two. When not sweating over page layout or photo editing, you can find him peering at the stars or growing vegetables.

WWII RECORDS RECOVERED. Germany has agreed to restitute an archive documenting Nazi persecution of Jehovah’s Witnesses, after the latter sued to recover it from Dresden’s Military History Museum, reports The New York Times. An amicable settlement finalized on November 20 concludes a years-long dispute about the rightful ownership of 31 documents and files related to the arrest and murder of the Kusserow family, who were Jehovah’s Witnesses. The archive in question “represents an invaluable part of the Witnesses’ cultural heritage and shines a light on the often overlooked abuses the group faced during World War II,” the Kusserow family stated. IN MEMORIAM. The artist and curator Tamlin Blake was killed in her home in Riebeek West, north of Cape Town, South Africa, and a suspect has been arrested, reported local media 2 Oceans Vibe. Blake’s body was found on November 22. “The attacker took several items before [he] fled,” said a spokesperson for the Western Cape regional police. The victim’s smartphone tracking device helped locate her stolen belongings, among items thought to have been worn by the attacker. The locally celebrated artist was also chief curator at Spier Arts Trust, a Cape Town-based organization that supports artists, helping them find opportunities to earn income, exhibit, and develop their practice, according to the website. Blake used textiles, found materials, and other mixed media, most recently consisting of tapestries woven from recycled hand-spun newspaper. “A prominent aspect of Blake’s work is her fascination with materials and manipulating new mediums in ways which take them past the merely decorative or prosaic. She was instrumental in developing beading techniques which are now used by various South African artists,” states her website.

Lévy Gorvy Dayan is bringing a Willem de Kooning priced at $32 million to Art Basel Miami Beach next week. [Artnet News]

After being featured in a Spanish television program about incredible archaeological discoveries by locals, an unearthed Roman mosaic was simply abandoned in the middle of a field, to the surprise of archaeologists. [El País]

Sotheby’s withdrew a Wade Guyton artwork estimated at $1 million to $1.5 million from its November 17 Contemporary Day Auction in New York because it was allegedly a fake, according to an unnamed source. [Artnet News]

Inconsistent requirements for and implementation of publicly supported artist housing around the US threaten the longevity and success of such initiatives. [The Art Newspaper]

FOOD FOR THOUGHT. About fifteen years ago, when Laila Gohar started making massive sculptures out of butter, she was something of an outlier, though the surrealists, Salvador Dalí in particular, had long looked at food as a playful window into the absurdity of daily life. In the Middle Ages, feasting royals were also known to host bacchanalian demonstrations of edible bounty turned into veritable sculptures. Now, according to The Guardian, Gohar is part of a trending wave of artists who use food as both main course and main medium. “I am interested in the rituals around eating and gathering, and in the way an ordinary thing can become something strange or theatrical when you change its scale, material or context,” said Gohar. “Food is one of the materials I work with, but I don’t really think of what I do as being separated into food, art, or design. They all feed into each other.”

#9052. Munch museum appoints Thorsten Sadowsky as new director

Sadowsky says he hopes to help further the Munch museum’s development “as an internationally minded, intellectually vibrant and socially relevant cultural institution“

The Munch museum in Oslo, dedicated to the work of the Modernist artist Edvard Munch, has appointed Thorsten Sadowsky to be its next director. Sadowsky, who joins Munch from Stiftung Schleswig-Holsteinische Landesmuseen Schloss Gottorf (Schleswig-Holstein State Museums Foundation Schloss Gottorf) in northern Germany, will begin his new role on 1 May 2027.

Sadowsky arrives with experience leading several prominent European institutions. His current position involves the management of multiple museums in the Schleswig-Holstein area, including the Museum of Art and Cultural History Schloss Gottorf and the Jewish Museum Rendsburg. Previously he has also directed the Museum der Moderne Salzburg, Museum Kunst der Westküste in Alkersum and the Kirchner Museum Davos, which is focused on the life and career of the German Expressionist Ernst Ludwig Kirchner.

“My experience at the Kirchner Museum Davos has taught me that the distinctive strength of a museum dedicated to a single artist can also be its greatest challenge,” Sadowsky tells The Art Newspaper. “Such a museum offers an exceptional opportunity to engage with an artist’s oeuvre with a degree of intensity and depth that is rarely possible in an art museum with a more broadly based collection. The challenge, however, is to ensure that the focus on a single artist does not lead to intellectual or curatorial narrowness.”

Sadowsky adds that his task is therefore “to continually open up new perspectives, reveal unexpected connections and bring the artist’s work into dialogue with other artistic practices, historical experiences and contemporary concerns”.

The Munch museum, which opened in a sprawling new home on Oslo’s Bjørvika waterfront in 2021, houses nearly 27,000 works of art by Munch. Alongside its permanent displays, the museum hosts a temporary exhibition programme that has brought Munch’s work into dialogue with that of contemporary artists such as Tracey Emin, Katherina Grosse and Alice Neel, as well as events such as concerts and conferences. It has welcome more than 700,000 visitors so far this year, according to a release.

Sadowsky tells The Art Newspaper that he first encountered Munch’s work at the Hamburger Kunsthaller, while he was a university student. The opportunity to direct the museum, he says, is exciting thanks to "the extraordinary richness of [Munch’s] artistic legacy. Beyond the familiar image of Munch as a painter of anxiety, loneliness and existential uncertainty, there is still much to discover. His work speaks equally of vitality, human relationships, our experience of nature and the social transformations of modernity.“

“Few artists have succeeded so convincingly in transforming individual experiences into images of universal human significance,” he adds. “In the realm of sculpture, Alberto Giacometti is another artist who achieved something similar.”

In his previous role as director of the Museum der Modern Salzburg, Sadowsky spoke about the importance of widening the scope of the programme and collection. He told the Austrian art magazine Parnass in 2022: “During my tenure as director, a major focus has been on broadening our perspective beyond the Western European canon and incorporating more postcolonial viewpoints.”

In his new role, Sadowsky says his immediate priority will be to “listen, to learn and to develop and deeper understanding“ of the institution and its people. “Over the coming years, I would like to further strengthen the Munch Museum as the world’s foremost centre of expertise on Edvard Munch, while continuing to develop it as an internationally minded, intellectually vibrant and socially relevant cultural institution,” he adds.

The Munch museum is owned by the city of Oslo. Mehmet Kaan Inan, Oslo’s vice mayor for culture and business development, says in a statement: “I am delighted that Munch [museum] will be led by a director with such strong international experience and outstanding expertise in the arts. Sadowsky has headed several highly respected art museums and has demonstrated a strong talent for audience development, collaboration, and engaging broad and diverse audiences. His exceptional interest in Edvard Munch’s artistic legacy also provides an excellent foundation for leading Munch [museum] into the future.”

Sadowsky takes over from Henrik Svalheim, who has served as interim director since Tone Hansen departed in October. Hansen left to lead Moderna Museet in Stockholm.

The Munch museum directorship runs as a six-year term, with the potential for one renewal.

#9051. Shigeru Ban unveils proposal for tent-like church in Rome

Images courtesy of Shigeru Ban Architects

A cross-shaped roof will mark the San Vincenzo de’ Paoli Church and Parish Complex in Rome, Italy, which Japanese studio Shigeru Ban Architects is designing with local architect Vittorio Petrucci.

The church will occupy a currently underused site in Ostia, a coastal neighbourhood for which the project is hoped to become an architectural landmark.

The San Vincenzo de’ Paoli Church and Parish Complex will be constructed with a frame of timber – Ban’s signature material – with a deliberately simple form that is intended to evoke a fabric tent.

According to Shigeru Ban Architects and Petrucci, the overarching goal is for the church to help establish a greater sense of community and place in the area, which they describe as having a “fragmented urban fabric”.

“We wanted to design a place of worship that also brings the whole community together,” said Ban.

“The timber structure expresses the idea of a tent, a simple, welcoming form that connects people with one another and with their surroundings. Through this project, we hope architecture can help create a new sense of belonging in the neighbourhood.”

Shigeru Ban Architects and Petrucci’s proposal was the winning entry of a competition for the church.

It is one of five winning designs selected as part of the New Churches Programme – an initiative led by the local church district, the Diocese of Rome, and the Italian Episcopal Conference, an assembly of Catholic bishops, to provide permanent homes for parish communities in the region.

As part of the project, four new churches will be built, while one existing parish complex will be extended.

The San Vincenzo de’ Paoli Church and Parish Complex will be built on a raised public plaza, with various parish facilities, community spaces and a priest’s residence embedded below.

Its key feature will be its angular roof, which is shaped like a cross but not immediately readable as one. This is modelled on a latent cross – a feature in sacred architecture, in which a cross shape is integrated in the spatial design, without being clearly visible.

Inside, the church will have a diamond-shaped plan, with large stained-glass windows positioned in the four cardinal directions. They will be triangular in shape and feature designs modelled on neighbourhood street art.

The project will be complete with a landscaped park, as well as various recreational and sports facilities, which the studios said will “create opportunities for social interaction and everyday activities”.

The San Vincenzo de’ Paoli Church and Parish Complex is not the first church project by Ban. Among his others is the landmark Cardboard Cathedral in New Zealand, which is formed of 98 cardboard tubes combined with wood and polycarbonate. We named it the most significant building of 2013 in our list of the 25 most significant buildings of the 21st century.

Other Italian church proposals recently featured on Dezeen include Stefano Boeri Architetti’s design for the Ambrosian Monastery in Milan, which will have a sail-like roof form.

If you regularly commuting to a studio or client meetings, a folding bike is a great investment in your health and wellbeing. It'll get you from the train station to your desk much faster than walking, then fold down small enough to tuck under it unobtrusively.

They aren't cheap, though, which is why the current crop of discounts caught my eye. Three of the most desirable compact bikes on the market right now are currently available at a Black Friday discount, with savings of up to £121.

We’re talking a budget-friendly pedal bike, a hand-built British design classic and an e-bike that's taking aim at the premium end of the market.

Motor: 250W rear hub, 40Nm, torque sensorBattery: 360Wh, USB-C chargingClaimed range: up to 120km (lowest assist level)Weight: 19.4kg with batteryFolded size: 62.5 x 37.4 x 67.3cmBrakes: hydraulic disc

Want an e-bike that folds? The Zip uses a patented triple fold and a torque sensor that kicks in as soon as you press on the pedals. Its battery charges over USB-C and can top up your phone in a pinch, and you get hydraulic disc brakes, which are rare at this price. Don't expect that 120km figure if you lean on full assist, though: one independent reviewer estimated 20 to 25 miles at the top setting. The Black Friday deal also includes free accessories, including a rear rack and mudguards, which ENGWE values at £108.

Frame: aluminiumGears: Shimano 6-speed with twist shifterWheels: 20inBrakes: V-brakesWeight: 11.54kgFolded size: 65 x 34 x 82cm

The Hit D6 is the cheapest and lightest bike on this list, making it a good choice for the first-time buyer. Its larger 20-inch wheels give a ride that feels closer to a standard bike, and six gears give you more help on hills than the Brompton's two. The trade-off is a bulkier fold, though it only takes three steps. A rack and mudguards come as standard, and Dahon throws in free shipping and a lifetime warranty.

Frame: steel, handmade in London Gears: 2-speed hub Wheels: 16in Brakes: rim (dual pivot calipers) Extras: mudguards included Warranty: 7-year frame

Brompton is the folding bike brand every other folding bike brand gets compared to. The 2-speed C Line is its simplest setup and its lightest steel bike, so it's well suited to flatter cities or riders with strong legs. It isn't electric and you only get rim brakes, but the fold is famously compact and the build quality is world-class. Note that Evans charges extra for delivery (£49.99) or collection in store (£19.99).

Two names have shaped the folding bike market more than any other. Dahon, which developed its folding system more than 30 years ago, built its reputation on affordable 20-inch-wheeled folders that ride much like a regular bike. Brompton, meanwhile, has spent more than four decades refining its 16-inch-wheeled design, which folds tighter than almost anything else and has become a design icon in its own right, with a price to match.

The newest development in the field is the electric folding bike, and that's where ENGWE comes in. Founded in Shenzhen, China in 2014, the brand first made its name with budget fat-tyre e-bikes, but it's now pushing into lighter, more commuter-friendly models.

To make things simple then: the Dahon Hit D6 is the light, low-cost way in to folding bikes. The Brompton C Line is the classic, if you can live with two gears and rim brakes. And the ENGWE Zip brings electric power to the small-wheeled format for less than the price of a pedal-only Brompton.

#9049. Meet Swedish Girls, Sabine Marcelis’s pick for Dezeen's 20x20 project

Sabine Marcelis has nominated Swedish Girls as a key name to watch over the next two decades for Dezeen’s 20×20 project sponsored by Kohler. In this interview, we learn why the design duo deliberately play into stereotypes.

The steady emergence of Swedish Girls has not been lost on prolific Dutch designer Marcelis, who nominated the collective as one of 20 names to watch in architecture and design over the next 20 years.

“I really like how they work with existing industrial production processes, yet the result very much speaks to the current culture,” Marcelis told Dezeen, explaining her selection.

Josefin Zachrisson and Mira Bergh run multidisciplinary studio Swedish Girls between Stockholm and Milan, creating furniture, installations and set design.

The duo met during their studies at Sweden’s Beckmans College of Design, where they graduated in 2019. They bonded over a desire to make work “without hierarchies” and maintain creative control of the studio’s output, which they prefer to call their ever-expanding “universe”.

The Big Bang for Swedish Girls was the selection of their collective’s tongue-in-cheek name, chosen after their first exhibition outing at Milan design week.

For experimental platform Alcova in 2021, Zachrisson and Bergh unveiled their ongoing metal rod Seats System project (pictured left).

Originally a single piece of modular seating without a defined front or back, the project has evolved into more metal pieces that follow the same design language, including a fruit bowl and a candle holder.

“We overheard people talking about our furniture, asking who made it, and others were like, ‘ah, it was those Swedish girls’, and we felt a bit belittled by it,” recalled Zachrisson. The duo had previously made work under their own names.

“The Swedish girl has obviously become a phenomenon,” added Bergh. “You know, blonde, sexy. But when we were talking about it, we also found it really funny because it’s so stereotypical. We thought we’d call ourselves Swedish Girls because everybody else was already calling us that.”

Humour is intrinsic to Zachrisson and Bergh’s interdisciplinary practice. Even their website, admired by Marcelis, was playfully designed as a Swedish Girls-branded Google search engine. It is meant to look like the internet itself, complete with mock web pages listing each of the collective’s projects.

“We got the idea when we launched the name Swedish Girls,” the pair explained.

“A professor from Beckmans called and said that we should change our name because when she Googled ‘Swedish Girls’, the search result was not exactly art and design,” they added.

“We thought that was so funny and decided to make Google about us instead of changing our name.”

Another of the duo’s wit-inflected projects is Only Fans, an installation presented at Gothenburg’s Röhsska design museum in 2024 during local music festival Way Out West.

Dubbed “a multidimensional art experience about fan culture” in all its forms, the installation included 25 electric fans, selected as a riff on adult content platform OnlyFans, where women are often the subject of scrutiny.

“The installation was interactive, so that visitors could stand in the middle of the fans in a hysterical storm,” said Bergh.

Our work is a lot of these really silly, stupid things. But it’s also layered with some seriousness, because the projects handle things that we are affected by and women are affected by in real life

Alongside the fans, the collective presented seven laser-cut steel chairs emblazoned with I <3 Swedish Girls, along with a fanzine and female mannequins wearing “metal merch” designed by Zachrisson and Bergh.

“Our work is a lot of these really silly, stupid things,” considered Zachrisson.

“But it’s also layered with some seriousness, because the projects handle things that we are affected by and women are affected by in real life,” she continued. “It feels like a way to approach it that makes it accessible.”

“Sometimes it’s hard because we get these questions like, ‘are you a feminist?'” added the designer. “But it’s inherently political to be a woman moving through the world. Our work is just reacting to our reality.”

The pair is keen to highlight that although they make furniture, “social values are always a starting point” for their projects.

“We really want to have a practice that feels purposeful,” said Zachrisson, considering the significance of partnering with institutions like design museums.

“We’ve realised that showing work in public spaces is the most important thing,” she continued.

“Especially because the materials and processes we use have become quite expensive. So we want to put our pieces in public spaces so that everyone can take part in some way.”

“You meet all different kinds of people, and we talk to them and grow from it,” added Bergh.

The hardest thing is to earn money. We’re adults, we’ve been doing this a long time. But we are still taken advantage of and expected to work for free or for very little money

Despite Swedish Girls’ various collaborations and recurring presence at Milan design week, seven years after leaving Beckmans, Bergh and Zachrisson continue to work in cafes and supermarkets to fund their design practice.

The duo are hyperaware of the difficulties faced by emerging creatives, especially those like themselves who, as they put it, “want to listen to your gut and be close to the process”.

“The hardest thing is to earn money,” said Bergh. “We’re adults, we’ve been doing this a long time. But we are still taken advantage of and expected to work for free or for very little money on very quick timelines. I feel like we should have more respect.”

“You don’t get paid in a way where you as two people can survive,” added Zachrisson. “But all these years of working and keeping our creative integrity is paying off in every way except financially.”

When it comes to building their studio, the designers consider themselves to be playing the long game.

“Long term, it’s an investment to do it this way because we have now created a context where we can feel freedom and gain respect, which is why we were so happy when Sabine nominated us,” said Zachrisson.

“You can measure success in so many different ways and with this we feel respected, and that is so valuable.”

The duo said funding that they won from Sweden’s Konstnärsnämnden arts council after graduating gave them a significant leg up when they were just starting out.

Zachrisson and Bergh are concerned that scholarships like theirs have been scarcer across Sweden in recent years thanks to the country’s right-wing administration, which came into power in 2022 and has only just been voted out of office.

“All the artists we have talked to have felt an extreme difference in that time,” noted Zachrisson. “The share of the total budget allocated to culture has not been this low in 26 years.”

Still, the pair are confident and excited about what’s to come.

“It comes in handy that we have a broad practice,” said Bergh. “We have plans for the future to make it easier for ourselves to be designers.”

“I like how they surprise with their projects and feel like we have only seen chapter one of their story,” concluded Marcelis. “And I can’t wait to discover the next chapter.”
