#8964. Sturdy backs J Cole’s set with neoclassical landmark from rapper’s hometown

A nine-metre-tall replica of a town hall in Fayetteville, North Carolina, takes centre stage at American rapper J Cole’s world tour set, which has been created by production company Sturdy.

The set for The Fall Off Tour was designed by Los Angeles-based Sturdy to realise J Cole’s ambition to take his hometown, Fayetteville – or “the ville”– “to the world”.

To do this, the studio drew on the historic, two-storey Market House building, which has stood as a local landmark in the city since 1832. Sturdy created a weathered, ivy-covered replica of the structure, which is neoclassical with gothic revival details.

“The Market House was chosen because it’s an iconic piece of architecture historically as well in the town that J Cole’s from,” Martinez told Dezeen.

“I think a big part of the intention is that he takes home with him wherever he goes; conceptually, the idea was to take ‘the ville’ to the world,” he continued.

“And what better way to do that than something that lives basically at the centre point of the entire city?”

Other nods to the rapper’s life in Fayetteville include the presence of a Honda Civic car, which Martinez describes as a “supporting actor in the show”.

Positioned in front of the building at centre stage, the car is supported on ties that allow it to be suspended above the stage during specific moments of the performance.

“The car is like a supporting actor in the show that adds a little bit of an authentic take to the performance,” he said.

“His fans know the black Civic, and, at least from my perspective, with this being The Fall Off, the car needs to have a place in the story. It’s part of ‘the ville’,” Martinez added.

The set was designed by Sturdy to be easily dismantled, shipped and rebuilt between shows across the US, Europe, South Africa, Australia and New Zealand.

This determined the scale and design of the neoclassical Market House replica, which stretches just over 15 metres and is composed of easy-to-assemble wood and metal components.

The materiality of the structure also allows for J Cole’s performance to extend to the building’s first-floor terrace.

Alongside the structure is a 23-metre-long walkway lined with grass, rocks and a tree stump that doubles as a seat for the artist.

“Any show that we are doing, especially of this scale, has to be designed from a ‘rigging perspective’ to how this thing breaks down,” Martinez explained.

“That all has to be thoroughly thought out because we’ve got to be able to have the proper Legos. We can’t really just show up and hope that it’s going to piece together,” he added.

Also contributing to the set is a large LED screen, which, according to Martinez, is used “rather sparingly” throughout the performances to bring the stage design to the fore.

“I think for a long stretch of time shows were just about crazy visuals and putting stuff on screens and just letting people see stuff moving in the background,” he said.

“We never use the entirety of the screen for the whole show,” Martinez continued. “It’s to add a little bit of depth to what we have going on scenically on stage.”

J Cole’s The Fall-Off World Tour has been running since July, with recent shows at London’s O2 Arena. The tour will end in December in Johannesburg, South Africa.

Other set designs recently featured on Dezeen include Dave’s London show, which Stufish illuminated with a laser-shooting piano.

#8963. Incline Walking vs. Running: What’s the Better Workout?

Incline walking and running are commonly framed as opposites: one is low impact, the other is high-intensity. But in reality, they’re both effective cardio options that challenge your body in distinct ways—from the muscles you recruit to the impact on your joints. Both workouts can boost your heart health, build endurance, and leave you seriously sweaty, but they place different demands on your body, according to Gab Reznik, CPT and Tone House coach. The question isn’t which is better across the board—it’s which is better for you depending on your goals.

Understanding those differences can help you decide which one deserves a spot in your fitness routine, or how to incorporate both.

At their core, incline walking and running share a common foundation: they get your body moving in a rhythmic, repetitive way that challenges your cardiovascular system.

“Any movement is better than no movement at all—whether that’s incline walking or running,” Reznik tells SELF. “They’re both effective at increasing blood flow, elevating heart rate, and improving overall aerobic capacity.” That means stronger heart and lung function over time—which are key markers of long-term health.

They also both demand muscular effort. Running requires you to generate power with every stride, while incline walking emphasizes controlled, deliberate steps against gravity (thanks to the incline). “Over time, the repetitive impact and loading can help strengthen joints and support long-term durability when done properly,” Reznik says.

While they may look similar on the surface, incline walking and running are different in two major ways: how hard they push your body, and how much stress they place on your joints.

Running is the higher-impact option. With each stride, your joints absorb roughly two to three times your body weight. That added force typically translates to higher intensity—and more calories burned per hour, Reznik explains.

Incline walking, on the other hand, keeps one foot on the ground at all times, reducing overall joint load. “Incline walking is more sustainable for longer durations,” Reznik says. “At the same fitness level, someone will typically be able to maintain an incline walk longer than a run due to the lower per-step demand.”

It’s easy to think of incline walking as purely cardio—but that’s only part of its benefits.

“Incline walking can absolutely build strength, just not in the same way as lifting weights,” Reznik says. Instead of maximizing muscle growth by picking up heavy weights, incline walking improves muscular endurance, particularly in the lower body (think: glutes, hamstrings, and calves).

The steeper the incline, the greater the challenge. And if you want to level up even more, try adding external load, like a weighted vest, Reznik suggests. “It can increase the strength stimulus without significantly increasing joint impact.”

Still, it’s important to keep your expectations realistic. If your goal is to build maximal strength or increase muscle size, traditional strength training should still be your primary focus.

One of the biggest misconceptions about incline walking is that it’s somehow inferior to running. Reznik is quick to shut that down.

“Walking isn’t less effective—it’s simply a different type of stimulus,” she says.

In fact, incline walking can be deceptively tough. Imagine this: a 15% incline at 3 mph for 30 minutes, without holding onto the treadmill. “That’s extremely challenging—even for a trained runner,” Reznik says.

Both workouts can improve cardiovascular fitness and support fat loss when programmed appropriately. The key is understanding that “effective” doesn’t mean “hardest”—it means the movement is aligned with your fitness goals.

If you’re aiming to maximize calorie burn in a shorter amount of time or really test your cardiovascular endurance, running may be the more efficient choice, Reznik says. Its higher intensity makes it ideal for pushing your limits.

But if you’re looking to reduce joint stress while still building aerobic fitness (and even some muscular endurance), incline walking may be the smarter pick. “If you treat them as complementary, you can unlock a higher level of performance and longevity,” Reznik says.

Deciding between incline walking and running ultimately comes down to three factors: your goals, your current fitness level, and what you actually enjoy enough to stick with.

Beginners might start with a light jog at a conversational pace or a slight incline (around 2% to 3%) at a comfortable walking speed, Reznik suggests. From there, it’s important to progress either the speed or incline, but not both at once.

“Incline walking isn’t the ‘easy’ option—it’s the smart option when used correctly,” Reznik says. “Running isn’t the ‘better’ option—it’s the specific option when it aligns with your goals.”

A well-rounded routine might include both: running for higher-intensity days when you want to challenge your cardio limits, and incline walking for longer, lower-impact sessions that still deliver a serious burn.

Ultimately, there’s no clear winner between incline walking and running because they aren’t rivals. Both movements can be tools for improving heart health, building endurance and strengthening key muscle groups. The better workout is the one that helps you move consistently and safely. And in many cases, the smartest approach isn’t choosing between them—it’s using both.

#8962. Nopales Benefits: Why You Might Add Cactus to Your Diet

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

Looking at a cactus with its threatening spikes and tough skin, you might not immediately think, “Yep, that’s a thing I could eat.” But guess what? Some forms of cacti are edible, tasty, and quite good for you!

Check out why it might be a good idea to pal around with nopales, the pads of the prickly pear cactus.

The nopal cactus, also known as the prickly pear or the opuntia, is a shrub-like, flowering cactus native to parts of Mexico, Arizona, the Mediterranean, Australia, and other desert regions. It might be recognized by its multitude of connected pads with flowering blooms. (A pad in bloom looks a little like a flat, green paw.)

Nopales flowers are filled with a viscous, seeded substance often used in jams, jellies, pies, cakes, and other sweets. But the stems, leaves, and entire pad (with spines removed, obvs) are also edible. Traditional Mexican preparations include boiling, grilling, and sautéing.

Science is still examining the possible benefits of nopales, so some touted wellness perks are fairly tentative. Here’s a look at what we know about these desert fruits.

Almost any time you see bright colors in edible fruits, it’s a sign they contain antioxidants. This is def true for Nopales!

Older studies have found that the fruit inside their flowers is rich in antioxidants like ascorbic acid, phenolics, and a mixture of betacyanin and betaxanthin. These compounds help fight inflammation by kicking harmful free radicals out of your cells.

Since they combat inflammation, the antioxidants in prickly pear could improve joint mobility. In a 2020 study, people who drank 3 ounces of prickly pear juice daily for 8 weeks had better range of motion and greater ease with daily activities than a control group who drank a placebo.

Research suggests nopales may help steady blood sugar. A 2014 study found that people with type 2 diabetes who ate nopales with a high-carb breakfast had significantly lower blood sugar and insulin levels compared to those who didn’t. However, this study only included 14 participants.

In 2019, a larger systematic review assessed the fruit’s potential for blood sugar regulation. While it found insufficient evidence to support using nopales to reduce the risk of type 2 diabetes, the authors noted it might significantly reduce blood glucose levels.

Showing your liver some love might involve adding nopales (or a glass of nopal juice) to your diet. According to research from 2023, this has to do with prickly pear’s effects on triglycerides. By helping reduce triglyceride accumulation, nopales could relieve stress on the liver.

Whether you’ve overdone it on booze or are down with a stomach bug, it’s important to rehydrate with a drink that contains electrolytes. Consider prickly pear juice as your back-on-the-wagon beverage. It’s got potassium, magnesium, and calcium to help rebalance your electrolyte levels.

If you can track down fresh nopales where you live, cooking it yourself is a fun (if somewhat complicated) way to take advantage of its benefits. If not, look for prickly pear products, such as juices, being sure to check for added sugars.

You can also take a supplement. Nopales supplements typically contain 500-650 milligrams (mg) per day.

While a prickly pear smoothie or nopales salad can be a healthy addition to your diet, consuming this cactus fruit may have some less-than-desirable side effects, like:

If you’re new to nopales, take it slow at first to see how your body responds.

Don’t let the “prickly” in prickly pear keep you away from this desert gem. When prepared correctly, nopales are unique, nutritious food. Check ’em out when your fruit basket needs something a little different.

#8961. RIBA president rejoins ARB register to restore architect title

The president of the Royal Institute of British Architects, Chris Williamson, has decided to renew his membership with the Architects Registration Board, nearly a year after terminating it.

In a LinkedIn post, Williamson said he was rejoining the Architects Registration Board’s (ARB) register because he no longer wanted “to face the prospect of legal action”.

Specifically, he said he feared the potential “legal proceedings and financial penalties” from referring to himself as an architect, which ARB does not permit if a person is unregistered.

Williamson’s post comes nearly a year after he revealed he was not going to renew his membership to draw attention to what he called the “absurdity of the current regulatory framework”.

This ARB framework currently only regulates the protected title “architect” and the competence of those on its register, meaning it does not oversee the competence of unregistered providers of architectural services.

His withdrawal from ARB last year aligned with the launch of a campaign by the Royal Institute of British Architects (RIBA) calling for a new regulatory model for UK architects.

Though he has now rejoined the ARB register, Williamson said his position on the need to reform remains unchanged.

“Today, I have decided to rejoin the ARB register,” he posted on LinkedIn on Friday.

“Over the last year, I have sat in meetings and roundtables with Ministers, MPs and Peers, spoken at party conferences and COP31, and had the pleasure of awarding the Stirling Prize,” he continued. “Throughout, I have felt the fear of legal proceedings and financial penalties all for referring to myself, in these settings, as an architect – something that’s so fundamental to my identity.”

Williamson, the co-founder of Weston Williamson + Partners, began his two-year term as president on 1 September 2025.

In the LinkedIn post – a shortened version of an open letter shared with RIBA members – he said he will now continue to “push for a stronger system” for regulation.

The current RIBA campaign calls for three steps to reform architects’ regulation, including repealing the Architects Act – a UK law that sets the framework for the regulation of the title architect, under which ARB is the regulator.

It also proposes new legislation outlining reserved activities, such as submitting full planning applications, and who can execute them. The final step calls for the introduction of a Built Environment Council to oversee the competence of individuals and companies working in the construction industry.

“I know my decision to return may surprise or disappoint some of you, particularly those who followed my lead,” concluded Williamson.

“I want to stress this is not a step backwards and it does not reflect a change in my views. In fact, the year I’ve spent outside of the Register has only cemented my commitment to reform,” he continued.

“While my title may change, RIBA’s campaign for regulatory reform will not. I will use my experience on both sides to push for a stronger system that protects what we call ourselves – and what we do.”

Williamson was selected as RIBA president in 2024. Prior to this, he held several roles within the RIBA, including the vice president international from 2017 to 2019.

In 2014, ARB gave Dezeen 14 days to amend an article describing John Pawson as an architect, claiming it was “in the public interest” for Dezeen to use an alternative description, as Pawson is not registered with the board.

#8960. designboom’s guide to miami art week 2026: what to see in and out of the fairs

explore must-see highlights of art basel miami beach, design miami, and other standout shows and events across the city.

Miami Art Week returns from November 30th to December 6th, 2026, bringing a packed program of art fairs, outdoor installations, exhibitions, and unexpected encounters across Miami and Miami Beach. This year, the city becomes a setting for everything from giant mirrored disco balls and interactive robots to surreal theatrical environments and public sculptures built for play.

Art Basel Miami Beach returns with a reconfigured fair and an expanded digital art program, while Design Miami explores the stories behind collectible objects through its curatorial theme, Unveiling. Beyond the convention center, the Miami Design District welcomes a series of interactive sculptural installations by Objects of Common Interest, and Faena Beach becomes a dance floor beneath a monumental mirrored sphere by Christopher Joshua Benton.

Meanwhile, CJ Hendry invites visitors into a swimming-pool-sized pit of oversized pills, Marcel Dzama brings his dreamlike universe to Lincoln Road, and Miami’s galleries and museums open new exhibitions. From established fairs to temporary interventions along the beachfront, here’s designboom’s guide to what to see across Miami Art Week 2026.

Art Basel Miami Beach returns to the Miami Beach Convention Center with 272 exhibitors from more than 40 countries and territories. For 2026, the fair introduces a reconfigured floor plan with a smaller overall footprint, longer sightlines, and established international galleries distributed throughout the space alongside younger exhibitors.

The fair’s main sectors bring together contemporary work and historic presentations, with Nova focusing on recently created pieces, Positions supporting emerging artists through solo booths, and Survey revisiting overlooked artistic practices. More than 30 galleries will participate for the first time, with a strong presence from Latin America and the Caribbean.

Zero 10, Art Basel’s platform dedicated to art of the digital era, returns with Generation, an exhibition curated by Karen Archey and Eli Scheinman. Featuring 19 projects, the presentation explores how digital technology is changing the ways art is made and experienced, with works by artists including Refik Anadol and Sarah Meyohas.

what: Art Basel Miami Beach when: December 4th — 6th, 2026 (VIP previews December 2–3) where: Miami Beach Convention Center, 1901 Convention Center Drive, Miami Beach, FL 33139

Design Miami returns for its 22nd edition with more than 75 exhibitors bringing together historic and contemporary collectible design. Under the direction of curator Charlene Prempeh, the 2026 fair follows the theme Unveiling, inviting visitors to look more closely at the cultural histories and making processes behind the objects on display.

The program spans established galleries and emerging practices, with furniture, lighting, and sculptural works presented alongside experimental installations. The fair’s Curio section provides a platform for more focused design presentations, while special projects and collaborations extend the program beyond the traditional gallery booth.

As one of the main events of Miami Art Week, Design Miami brings together designers, collectors, and galleries working across different generations of material experimentation and craftsmanship.

what: Design Miami when: December 2nd — 6th, 2026 (invitation-only previews December 1st and 2nd) where: Convention Center Drive and 19th Street, Miami Beach, FL

Untitled Art celebrates its 15th Miami Beach edition with more than 170 galleries and nonprofit organizations representing 36 countries and territories. The fair returns to its beachfront pavilion along Ocean Drive, offering a curated selection of contemporary art with an emphasis on emerging practices and independent galleries.

The 2026 edition features five sectors: Main, Artist Spotlight, Nest, Non-Profit, and Special Projects. Artist Spotlight, curated by Agustina Ferreyra, brings together focused solo presentations, while Nest, curated by Willem Molesworth, explores collaboration and exchange across East Asia and the wider international art scene.

With 53 first-time exhibitors joining the program, the fair continues to create space for younger galleries alongside established international participants.

what: Untitled Art when: December 2nd — 6th, 2026 where: Ocean Drive and 12th Street, Miami Beach, FL

The New Art Dealers Alliance returns to Ice Palace Studios for the 24th edition of NADA Miami, bringing together 135 exhibitors from 63 cities and 27 countries.

Known for its focus on independent galleries and emerging artistic practices, NADA presents work from both established and younger art spaces. Its relatively informal setting offers an opportunity to discover artists working across painting, installation, sculpture, and experimental media, with presentations that often take a more exploratory approach than those found at the larger international fairs.

The event occupies Ice Palace Studios in downtown Miami, with exhibitions and programming extending into its outdoor areas.

what: NADA when: December 1st — 5th, 2026 where: Ice Palace Studios, 1400 North Miami Avenue, Miami, FL 33136

Art Miami returns to its waterfront pavilion at One Herald Plaza with an international selection of modern and contemporary art. One of Miami’s longest-running art fairs, the event brings together established galleries presenting works from the 20th and 21st centuries.

The fair spans painting, sculpture, photography, and installation, with a program that moves between historically significant artists and contemporary practices. Alongside conventional gallery presentations, visitors can expect individual artist projects and interactive installations, including a new felt environment by British artist Lucy Sparrow.

Located in downtown Miami, the fair takes place alongside its sister event CONTEXT Art Miami, allowing visitors to move between the two exhibitions.

what: Art Miami when: December 2nd — 6th, 2026 where: One Herald Plaza, NE 14th Street, Miami, FL 33132

Running alongside Art Miami, CONTEXT Art Miami returns to One Herald Plaza with a focus on emerging and mid-career contemporary artists. The sister fair brings together 75 international galleries presenting new work and curated solo exhibitions.

Established in 2012, CONTEXT offers a platform for galleries working with younger artists and those developing new approaches to familiar media. The fair also features installations and projects created specifically for the event, offering visitors a view of contemporary practices beyond the more established market represented at Art Miami.

what: CONTEXT Art Miami when: December 1st — 6th, 2026 where: CONTEXT Art Miami Pavilion, One Herald Plaza, NE 14th Street, Miami, FL 33132

Amsterdam-based Studio DRIFT brings Murmuring Minds to Art Basel Miami Beach’s Zero 10 sector, presented with the digital art platform TAEX. The installation transforms an arena of autonomous robotic blocks into a responsive environment, with their movement shifting according to the actions of visitors.

Entering the space, one person at a time can influence the robots as they move collectively, follow a lead, or behave according to patterns inspired by wind and natural swarms. The project draws on DRIFT’s long-running research into collective behavior, particularly the coordinated movements of birds and other living systems.

The presentation also includes Coded Nature, an interactive digital series in which algorithmically generated swarms respond to visitors’ gestures. Together, the works examine how individual actions influence the behavior of larger systems.

what: Studio DRIFT, Murmuring Minds and Coded Nature when: December 4th — 6th, 2026 (VIP previews December 2–3) where: Art Basel Miami Beach, Zero 10, Miami Beach Convention Center

At Art Basel’s Zero 10, Sarah Meyohas presents Phase Transition, a new installation of organic, sculptural forms that appear to communicate through movement and sound. Presented by Boesky Gallery, the work brings together magnetized liquid, algorithmic systems, and synthesizers to create a strange conversation among objects.

The forms rest on mesh pedestals or hang from suspended wires. Cutout windows reveal glass tanks filled with ferrofluid, a liquid containing magnetic particles that shift in response to programmed magnets. These movements are translated into sound, allowing each sculpture to participate in an ongoing exchange.

Their rounded, bodily shapes reference biological growth and transformation, while their mechanical conversations raise questions about intelligence and communication beyond human language. The installation extends Meyohas’ interest in the relationship between organic life and emerging technologies.

what: Sarah Meyohas: Phase Transition when: December 4th — 6th, 2026 (VIP previews December 2nd — 3rd) where: Art Basel Miami Beach, Zero 10, Miami Beach Convention Center

During Miami Art Week this December, artist Derrick Adams and the LEGO Group will bring a nine-foot unicorn pool float to Miami Beach. Built from LEGO bricks, the oversized figure will sit at the center of Pool Party, a colorful installation at Avant Gallery inside 1111 Lincoln Road. The project takes Adams’ long-running Floaters series, with its images of Black people at leisure, into an entirely different medium.

On December 3rd and 4th, visitors will have a hand in creating the artwork themselves. Adams and the LEGO team will invite the public to help assemble parts of the installation, ahead of its completed unveiling on December 5th. The two-day community build is part of The Art of Building, a participatory experience organized during Miami Art Week — RSVP here!

what: Derrick Adams x LEGO: The Art of Building when: December 3rd — 4th, 2026 (completed installation reveal December 5th) where: Avant Gallery, 1111 Lincoln Road, Miami Beach, Florida

Japanese artist Tadashi Kawamata brings a site-specific installation to Collins Park in collaboration with Maison Ruinart during Art Basel Miami Beach. Part of the champagne house’s ongoing Conversations with Nature program, the work draws on Kawamata’s observations of Ruinart’s historic vineyards in France.

Known for his temporary architectural constructions made from lightweight materials, Kawamata approaches installation as a process of responding to a place. His Miami commission continues that interest through a large-scale structure that invites visitors to reconsider their relationship with the surrounding environment.

what: Tadashi Kawamata x Maison Ruinart when: December 3rd — 6th, 2026 where: Collins Park, Miami Beach, FL

Dutch designer Iris van Herpen brings her collaboration with Maison Perrier-Jouët to Design Miami, following its presentation in Tokyo and Paris earlier this year. The project grew from her selection as the inaugural recipient of the Perrier-Jouët Design for Nature Award.

Drawing on cymatics, the study of how vibrations produce visible patterns, van Herpen translated signals associated with the living ecosystem of the champagne house’s vineyards into sculptural forms.

The resulting creations include Symphonic Bloom, a one-of-a-kind artwork made from recycled golden metal and silk surrounding a historic champagne bottle, and Symphonic Life, a limited series of sculptural sleeves adorned with gold. The pieces carry van Herpen’s interest in natural structures into the scale of collectible objects.

what: Iris van Herpen x Maison Perrier-Jouët when: December 2nd — 6th, 2026 where: Design Miami, Convention Center Drive and 19th Street, Miami Beach

British artist Lucy Sparrow returns to Art Miami with The Money Laundry, an interactive installation that transforms a familiar laundromat into a shop filled with handmade felt objects.

Among the colorful boxes of detergent and cleaning supplies, visitors will find painted felt banknotes, imitation luxury watches, and passports created by the artist. Sparrow will also exchange $100 in real money for a bundle of felt currency carrying a fictional value of $600.

An on-site photo booth allows guests to have their own felt passports painted live, extending the artist’s ongoing interest in consumer culture and the objects through which people assign value.

what: Lucy Sparrow: The Money Laundry when: December 1st — 6th, 2026 where: Art Miami, Booth AM207, One Herald Plaza, Miami

Artist Christopher Joshua Benton transforms Faena Beach into a temporary dance floor with A Lore Supreme, a monumental kinetic sculpture that reimagines the disco ball as a map of Miami’s cultural history.

The mirrored sphere rises 27 feet above the sand and stretches 44 feet across. Its surface is composed of around 7,000 reflective facets, which move with the wind and scatter images of the surrounding beach.

Partially embedded in the ground, the sculpture becomes both a gathering place and a setting for music and performance.

Drawing on research into Miami’s musical communities, Benton incorporates recorded conversations and sound from local DJs and musicians. The installation traces the influence of African, Caribbean, and Latin American cultures on the city’s music, turning the beach into an open-air space for listening and dancing.

what: Christopher Joshua Benton: A Lore Supreme when: December 1st — 6th, 2026, noon-9 p.m. where: Faena Beach, 3201 Collins Avenue, Miami Beach, FL 33140

The Miami Design District’s 11th Annual Design Commission has been awarded to Objects of Common Interest, the New York- and Athens-based studio founded by Eleni Petaloti and Leonidas Trampoukis.

Titled Out of This World: A Field of Conditions, the installation places six abstract sculptures throughout the neighborhood. Some release clouds of vapor into the Miami air, while others rotate when touched or distort their surroundings through reflective surfaces. A marble-and-resin pyramid produces sound that becomes audible only when visitors approach.

Developed through the studio’s ongoing experiments with resin, marble, and movement, the commission extends into Design Miami with a companion installation, Out of This World: A Certain Attraction. There, a concealed sculptural object responds to the presence of visitors, shifting to reveal fragmented reflections of those who enter.

what: Objects of Common Interest, Out of This World: A Field of Conditions when: during Miami Art Week 2026 (exact opening date to be confirmed) where: various locations throughout the Miami Design District, Miami, FL

Artist Marcel Dzama brings his distinctive universe of masked figures and theatrical imagery to Miami Beach with Who Loves the Moon?, an immersive installation presented by Capital One and The Cultivist.

The experience begins with a giant Moon that opens its mouth to welcome visitors inside. From there, guests move through a series of environments incorporating illuminated optical works, puppetry, and imagery drawn from Dzama’s paintings and films.

The journey culminates in a theatrical landscape with checkerboard floors and towering palms. By day, visitors can play chess and explore tarot and astrological readings. Evening programming introduces music and performances by Miami City Ballet, bringing the artist’s imagined world into motion.

what: Marcel Dzama: Who Loves the Moon? when: December 1st — 4th, 2026 (free public viewing December 3rd — 4th) where: 434 Lincoln Road, Miami Beach, FL 33139

Australian artist CJ Hendry joins Salon 94 Design to bring PASTEL to the Miami Design District, transforming thousands of oversized pills into an immersive landscape of color.

The installation revisits Hendry’s earlier bead-filled environment, this time replacing the familiar spherical forms with sculptural vitamins, supplements, and prescription pills. Visitors can enter the swimming-pool-sized pit, sift through the colorful objects, and assemble their own playful prescriptions.

Through the oversized forms, Hendry turns familiar products associated with health and self-optimization into objects for interaction and play.

what: CJ Hendry x Salon 94 Design: PASTEL Miami when: November 30th — December 20th, 2026 where: 3925 North Miami Avenue, Miami, FL 33127

At The Ritz-Carlton, South Beach, American artist Rachel Lee Hovnanian presents The Perfect Trade-Off, a solo exhibition exploring how technology has changed the ways people spend time together.

In the hotel’s Art Deco lobby, Dinner for Ten stages an elaborate meal with ten places at the table. Nine chairs are occupied by monitors depicting individuals absorbed in their phones, leaving a single empty seat for visitors. As the feast deteriorates, the work considers what happens to shared rituals when attention turns toward digital devices.

The exhibition extends onto the beachfront with Poor Teddy in Memoriam, a monumental bronze teddy bear surrounded by flowers. Elsewhere, a vintage three-wheeled Piaggio Ape has been transformed into a functioning phone-charging station, bringing Hovnanian’s examination of our relationship with technology into a familiar, everyday encounter.

what: Rachel Lee Hovnanian: The Perfect Trade-Off when: December 1st — 8th, 2026 where: The Ritz-Carlton, South Beach, 1 Lincoln Road, Miami Beach, FL 33139

Argentine artist and designer Andrés Reisinger brings his dreamlike architectural imagery into physical space with Do You Dream In Color?, a property-wide exhibition at Andaz Miami Beach Resort & Spa.

Known for his surreal digital environments and all-pink architectural takeovers, Reisinger will transform parts of the hotel through immersive installations and digital artworks. At the entrance, one of his signature draped interventions will cover the architecture in flowing fabric-like forms, while more digital works appear throughout Bar Centro and the hotel’s screens.

The exhibition is presented with ArtRepublic, and brings Reisinger’s digitally conceived aesthetic into an environment that visitors can experience in-person.

what: Andrés Reisinger: Do You Dream In Color? when: December 1st — 6th, 2026 where: Andaz Miami Beach Resort & Spa, 4041 Collins Avenue, Miami Beach, FL 33140

Greek designer Natalia Triantafylli presents Under the Libra Sun at Villa Paula in Miami’s Little Haiti neighborhood, marking her first major exhibition and largest-scale work to date. Presented by The Future Perfect, the collection takes inspiration from the historic villa’s original tiles and gardens, with pieces that reinterpret Greek and Victorian ornament through bright colors and floral patterns.

Triantafylli hand-sculpts forms in clay before scanning them and combining them with 3D-printed counterparts. The collection includes two monumental porcelain chandeliers, decorative mirrors, column-capital tables and stools, and her first upholstered pieces. Several works are developed with her partner, artist Andrew Pierce Scott, whose blackened steel structures contrast with her richly patterned ceramics. The pieces are bolted together rather than glued to leave their construction visible.

what: Natalia Triantafylli: Under the Libra Sun, presented by The Future Perfect when: opening November 30th, 2026 where: Villa Paula, 5811 North Miami Avenue, Miami, FL 33127

Bosnian artist Radenko Milak presents Algorithms for the Future at Piero Atchugarry Gallery in Miami, his first solo exhibition in the city. Curated by Claire Breukel, the show brings together hyperrealistic black-and-white watercolors that examine how technology shapes our memories of the past and visions of the future. Drawing from archival photography, science fiction, and architecture, Milak combines familiar imagery with imagined scenarios, from Edward Hopper’s solitary figures to futuristic skyscrapers filled with surveillance equipment.

Among the works is White Noise (2026), which merges a warped urban tower with vintage recording devices, and Ghost Game, a series of 23 paintings tracing the history of artificial intelligence through mathematics, cinema, and popular culture. Each image is painted by hand with near-photographic precision, a deliberately slow process that contrasts with the speed of algorithmically generated pictures. The works question what happens when machines begin to determine how history is represented and remembered.

what: Radenko Milak: Algorithms for the Future, curated by Claire Breukel when: November 29th, 2026 — April 18, 2027 where: Piero Atchugarry Gallery, 5520 NE 4th Avenue, Miami, FL 33137

Design Hotels teams up with Play-Doh for Designed to Play, a five-day program at The Shelborne by Proper in Miami Beach during Miami Art Week 2026. At its center is an installation by Copenhagen-based Helle Mardahl Studio, created in collaboration with Hasbro’s new Blooms by Play-Doh collection. The project marks an unusual moment for the familiar modeling compound, which has introduced its first line developed specifically for adults in the brand’s 70-year history.

Throughout the week, visitors can experiment with the colorful material in hands-on workshops and create their own sculptural bouquets. The hotel will also host morning conversations on creativity and design, while New York’s Pawn Chess Club brings custom chessboards and open games to the space. The program takes a playful approach to the usual Miami Art Week schedule, with opportunities to make something, try a new game, or simply spend an afternoon experimenting.

what: Design Hotels x Play-Doh, Designed to Play, featuring Helle Mardahl Studio when: December 2nd — 6th, 2026 where: The Shelborne by Proper, 1801 Collins Avenue, Miami Beach, FL 33139

Miami’s Wynwood Arts District welcomes Grotto Baths on December 1, a 7,500-square-foot social bathhouse that brings contemporary art into the centuries-old tradition of communal bathing. Designed by Antoinette Marie Johnson in collaboration with Stokes Architecture + Design, the interiors draw from Brazilian modernism, with curved archways, geometric tile patterns, and bursts of orange and blue against natural stone and travertine. Visitors move between thermal pools and cold plunges, while a 30-person cedar sauna hosts guided rituals accompanied by aromatic steam.

Art plays a central role in the new space. Miami-based artist Emmett Moore has created site-specific sculptures and custom benches using reclaimed materials inspired by South Florida’s limestone and mid-century breeze-block architecture. Works by Papou appear in the lobby, and an exterior mural by Mandy Ann takes inspiration from water. The phone-free bathhouse also includes a garden café, with special food and drinks inspired by Moore’s installations planned for Miami Art Week.

what: Grotto Baths, featuring site-specific installations by Emmett Moore when: Opens December 1st, 2026, for members (day-pass access begins December 7th) where: Grotto Baths, 325 NW 28th Street, Miami, FL 33127

At Nobu Hotel Miami Beach, Japanese artist and ceramic conservator Naoko Fukumaru presents a collection of works exploring the centuries-old practice of kintsugi, the repair of broken ceramics using lacquer and gold.

Presented in collaboration with The Morikami Museum and Japanese Gardens, the lobby exhibition brings together ceramic objects that have been broken, discarded, or altered through firing. Fukumaru reconstructs their forms using natural urushi lacquer and 23.5-karat gold, leaving visible lines that trace the histories of the objects.

With more than three decades of experience in ceramic conservation, the Kyoto-born artist approaches repair as an opportunity to give damaged objects a new visual identity.

what: Naoko Fukumaru: The Kintsugi Art of Naoko Fukumaru when: November 25th — December 7th, 2026 where: Nobu Hotel Miami Beach, 4525 Collins Avenue, Miami Beach, FL 33140

Miami’s Little River neighborhood welcomes a new cultural space with the opening of Mitrani Art, a multidisciplinary center dedicated to photography, video art, and film.

Founded by sisters Dina and Rhonda Mitrani and designed by R&R Studios, the project transforms a former mechanic shop into galleries and artist studios, with a screening room and outdoor courtyard. The opening marks a new chapter for the sisters, who previously operated the Mitrani Warehouse in Wynwood.

The inaugural exhibition, ReExposures: The Magic Within, brings together artists who have contributed to their programs over the years. Works range from large-scale photographic experiments to video installations, including a monumental photogram by Roberto Huarcaya and Antonia Wright’s video Suddenly We Jumped, in which the artist breaks through panes of glass.

what: Mitrani Art, ReExposures: The Magic Within when: Opening November 30th, 2026 (6-9 p.m. reception) where: Mitrani Art, 7325 North Miami Avenue, Miami, FL 33150

The Bass in Miami Beach presents a season of exhibitions that bring visitors into direct contact with the works on view, from interactive environments to sculptural installations.

In the museum’s Rotunda, Argentine artist Amalia Pica presents Lecturas Posibles, an almost two-dimensional library where surfaces become chalkboards. Visitors are invited to write and draw across the installation, creating an evolving collection of marks and messages.

Elsewhere, Japanese artist Yuko Mohri’s Unviolated Imperfection explores everyday objects through unpredictable mechanical systems, while architecture and design duo Pedro y Juana transform an interior with patterned surfaces and custom furniture for Aquí. Their richly colored environment draws on Miami’s subtropical setting, inviting visitors to spend time within the installation.

what: The Bass 2026-2027 exhibition season, featuring Amalia Pica, Yuko Mohri, and Pedro y Juana when: exhibitions on view throughout Miami Art Week 2026 where: Bass Museum of Art, 2100 Collins Avenue, Miami Beach, FL 33139

LVMH The Studio Miami returns for its sixth edition, bringing a five-day program of contemporary art and creative workshops to the Miami Design District.

The pop-up gallery presents works by ten artists working across painting, sculpture, textiles, photography, and digital media. Participating artists include Cavier Coleman, Glenneisha Darkins, Jay Chung, and Kristen White, alongside others exploring identity and cultural history through different materials.

Alongside the exhibition, visitors can attend public conversations and craftsmanship demonstrations organized with artisans and creative partners from Louis Vuitton, Tiffany & Co., and TAG Heuer.

what: LVMH The Studio Miami 2026 when: December 2nd — 6th, 2026, 11 a.m.-4 p.m. where: Palm Court Event Space, 140 NE 39th Street, 3rd Floor, Miami, FL 33137

The Craig Robins Collection unveils its 2026-2027 rehang, Real Shadows, featuring more than 300 works of modern and contemporary art and design.

Presented at Dacra’s headquarters in the Miami Design District, the exhibition brings together pieces by John Baldessari, Charles Ray, and Marlene Dumas, alongside recent acquisitions by artists including Alex Da Corte and Lauren Halsey.

Taking its title from Baldessari’s Tetrad Series (1999), the exhibition explores the persistence of images through painting and sculpture. The presentation also incorporates significant design objects by Zaha Hadid, Jean Prouvé, and Ron Arad, reflecting the collection’s long-standing relationship between art and furniture.

what: Craig Robins Collection: Real Shadows when: 2026-2027; Wednesdays-Fridays, noon-4 p.m., by appointment where: Dacra Headquarters, 3841 NE 2nd Avenue, Miami, FL 33137

El Espacio 23 in Miami’s Allapattah neighborhood presents Nothing Is Linear: Relations Across Latin America and Its Diasporas, a new exhibition drawn from the Jorge M. Pérez Collection. Bringing together more than 130 works by 120 artists, the exhibition examines the region’s shifting cultural identities through migration and shared histories. Curated through a collaboration between Anelys Alvarez, Patricia Hanna, Taiyana Pimentel, and Patrick Charpenel, the presentation moves between figurative art, political expression, and abstraction.

Among the works is José Carlos Martinat’s kinetic sculpture Manifestos, whose moving pendulums and speakers broadcast historical art manifestos in their original languages. Elsewhere, Hernan Bas revisits Miami’s brief snowfall in 1977, while works by Julio Le Parc and Adrián Villar Rojas explore different approaches to visual language. Across four interconnected sections, the exhibition considers Latin America as a network of relationships that extends far beyond geographical borders.

what: Nothing Is Linear: Relations Across Latin America and Its Diasporas when: November 19th, 2026 — August 14th, 2027 where: El Espacio 23, 2270 NW 23rd Street, Miami, FL 33142

Jeffrey Deitch presents Ensalada Mixta, an exhibition of work by Swiss artist Urs Fischer in the Miami Design District.

The presentation explores Fischer’s approach to transforming familiar objects through unexpected materials and changes in scale. Working across sculpture and design, the artist draws on industrial processes and common domestic forms, using materials including steel, epoxy, and electrical components.

The exhibition continues Fischer’s long-running interest in the relationship between art objects and the everyday things that surround them, bringing his playful visual language into a temporary gallery setting during Miami Art Week.

what: Urs Fischer: Ensalada Mixta, presented by Jeffrey Deitch when: November 30th — December 23rd, 2026 where: 45 NE 39th Street, Miami, FL 33137

At the Institute of Contemporary Art, Miami, Basquiat. A Hidden World offers a new perspective on Jean-Michel Basquiat’s paintings through his little-known use of ultraviolet-reactive materials.

Curated by Dieter Buchhart and Anna Karina Hofbauer, the exhibition brings together four works, including Untitled (Orange Sports Figure) (1982), Emblem (1984), Cash Crop (1984), and O.M.R.A.V.S. (1984).

Under ultraviolet light, words and markings hidden within the surfaces become visible. In Emblem, the repeated phrase ‘invisible men’ appears beneath the familiar composition, revealing an additional layer of Basquiat’s visual language.

what: Basquiat: A Hidden World when: November 29th, 2026 — February 12th, 2027 where: ICA Miami Expansion Space, 23 NE 41st Street, Miami, FL 33137

Indian artist Subodh Kerkar brings The Ocean Odyssey to Miami Beach as a free public performance presented by REEFLINE in collaboration with Andaz Miami Beach Resort & Spa.

The site-specific project brings together more than 50 community participants and dancers from Miami City Ballet, with choreography developed in collaboration with Durante Verzola.

Taking place directly on the beachfront, the performance uses movement to explore the relationship between people and marine environments. The ocean becomes the setting for a temporary gathering that connects contemporary art with Miami’s coastal landscape.

what: Subodh Kerkar: The Ocean Odyssey, presented by REEFLINE when: December 1st, 2026, 4:30-6 p.m. where: Andaz Miami Beach Resort & Spa beachfront, 4041 Collins Avenue, Miami Beach, FL 33140

#8959. Ultimate Guide to 4A Hair: Care Tips, Styles, and Maintenance

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

Understanding your hair type is key to achieving healthy, luscious curls. Hair types range from 1 to 4 — straight, wavy, curly, and coily — with type 4 being the curliest. Type 4A hair has a fine texture and loose curl pattern, forming springy coils that need special care to stay healthy and vibrant.

Knowing your hair type helps determine the best hair care routine. Caring for 4A hair is essential, whether you’re dealing with dryness or breakage or want to define your curls.

Let’s dive into the world of 4A hair and discover how to keep those curls popping.

Alright, curl friends, let’s break it down. Hair type falls into four main categories:

Now, Type 4 hair is where things get seriously curly and coily. Within this category, we’ve got subtypes A, B, and C,

which refer to the width and density of your curls.

So, what’s the deal with 4A hair? 4A hair is the queen of the fine, loose curl pattern. It forms tight, springy coils that are like tiny, perfect S-shapes. These curls are less dense than their 4B and 4C cousins, making them more defined and delicate. Think of 4A hair as the Goldilocks of coily hair — not too tight, not too loose, but just right.

Your hair is unique and gorgeous, but it requires a bit of extra TLC to keep it looking its best. Here’s a straightforward guide to keeping your 4A hair moisturized, healthy, and thriving:

4A hair tends to be dry as its coily structure makes it difficult for natural oils to travel down the hair shaft. Keeping it moisturized is essential, so incorporate a good leave-in conditioner into your daily shampooing routine. Use deep conditioning treatments weekly to replenish moisture and strengthen your curls.

Don’t forget scalp care, too! For maximum hydration, look for products with ingredients like shea butter, coconut oil, and glycerin.

4A hair is prone to tangles, so detangle gently to avoid breakage. Use a wide-tooth comb or your fingers to work through knots carefully. Start from the ends and work your way up to the roots, and always detangle when your hair is wet and coated with conditioner to provide slip and minimize damage.

Heat styling tools can cause significant damage to 4A hair, leading to dryness, breakage, and loss of curl pattern. Minimize the use of blow dryers, flat irons, and curling wands. If you use heat, always apply a heat protectant spray first to shield your hair from high temperatures.

Pro tip: To maintain the health of your curls, opt for air-drying or styles that don’t require heat.

Protective styles like braids, twists, and buns can help reduce manipulation and minimize breakage. These styles tuck away your ends, protecting them from friction and environmental damage.

Cotton pillowcases cause friction, which leads to frizz and breakage, especially for 4A hair. Switching to satin or silk pillowcases instead helps mai

ntain your curl pattern and prevent tangles.

Regular trims are crucial for keeping 4A hair healthy and preventing split ends from traveling up the hair shaft. Aim to trim your hair every 8-12 weeks to remove damaged ends and keep your curls looking fresh and vibrant.

Yes, 4A hair is curly and falls under the coily category. It features tight, springy curls that form an S-shape.

To determine your hair type, look at the curl pattern, texture, and density. 4A hair has a loose curl pattern with fine, springy coils, while 4B and 4C hair have tighter curls. 3C hair is curly but not as tight as Type 4.

Washing once a week or every two weeks is generally sufficient for 4A hair. Overwashing can strip the hair of its natural oils.

Regular trims every 8-12 weeks help keep 4A hair healthy by removing split ends and preventing breakage.

Taking care of your 4A hair isn’t rocket science, but it does need a little know-how and the right tools.

Love those natural curls — keep them hydrated, avoid excessive heat, and give them some nighttime TLC.

#8958. IKEA's Color of the Year "unexpectedly fits in"

Photography courtesy of IKEA (unless stated otherwise)

Swedish retailer IKEA has unveiled its prediction for 2027’s Color of the Year – a dark, reddish-purple shade called Wild Fig.

Although revealed by IKEA US as part of its 2027 Style Guide, keen eyes would’ve already seen the shade pop up earlier this year in the sell-out floor lamp created by Dutch designer Lex Pott for IKEA’s PS Collection.

The company describes Wild Fig as “a deep, botanical shade with a rich purple tone”, although in certain lights, it looks closer to an earthy oxblood red.

“Full of character and the unexpected, it brings depth and a daring mindset to everyday spaces,” said Abbey Stark, home furnishing direction leader at IKEA US.

Used across furnishings and accessories, it can provide a subtle touch of colour without being overly aggressive, especially paired with warm woods and neutral shades, IKEA US suggests.

But the company equally pictures it being splashed across entire walls and argues it “unexpectedly fits in” with even brighter colours like baby pink and electric blue – IKEA US’s previous colours of the year.

The company’s Style Guide also pulled out a number of other interior design trends to look out for in 2027, including pattern clashing and Japandi minimalism.

Interior designers have already started making liberal use of Wild Fig, as seen in Note Design Studio’s scheme for the Lammhults showroom in Stockholm, where it blankets walls, floors and ceilings in the entrance, as well as an entire kitchen.

Other predictions for 2027’s colour of the year are set to start rolling in any minute, with Pantone’s set to be unveiled at the start of December.

Paint brand Dulux got ahead of the game when it named a muted green called Soulful Sage as its contender in September.

Some interiors industry insiders, including Dezeen columnist Michelle Ogundehin, have argued at least since the end of the pandemic that “it’s time to reconsider the whole colour of the year carnival”, which was originally invented as a marketing stunt for Pantone’s colour-matching system, much like the Michelin Guide was invented to sell more tyres.

Photography courtesy of IKEA (unless stated otherwise)

#8957. How to Have Great Sex After 60, According to Experts

There’s a common assumption that great, adventurous sex is a young person’s game—and with age, it fades into something boring, nonexistent, or just…not worth the effort.

Growing up, Karen Bigman fell for the propaganda. “But recently, I’ve done it in restaurant bathrooms,” Bigman, a 62-year-old certified sex educator, tells SELF, before listing off other examples of her scandalous escapades. “I’ve spontaneously met up in hotel rooms when the kids were at home. We even pulled over next to a Duane Reade [convenience store], under the fluorescent lamp, to do it in the back seat of his car.”

To be clear, sex isn’t always this spontaneous for Bigman. But in both her own life and her work with clients, she insists sex in this stage of life isn’t just happening: It’s getting better. For some, it’s even kinkier—though it’s a reality you rarely hear about and probably don’t want to imagine your parents or grandparents doing.

The fear that your sex life dies with age doesn’t come from nowhere. Bodies change. Menopause (which typically starts in a person’s 40s or 50s) can bring on a slew of symptoms like vaginal dryness or painful sex. Hormonal shifts can lower libido across all sexes. Energy levels fluctuate—and acting out on desires that once felt automatic may now require more effort, communication, and patience.

Still, none of this has to spell the end of a satisfying bedroom life, according to both sex therapists and real people enjoying sex after 60. Here’s how they maintain the spark—and the small shifts they say make the biggest differences.

Vaginal dryness is one of the most common physical changes that comes with aging—and it’s why many people assume getting frisky in this stage will be uncomfortable or painful.

However, there are plenty of expert-recommended products designed to help, and lube is one of the most effective and underrated. “Put it on before you start and have it at the ready during sex,” Bigman, who also shares her advice on her Taboo to Truth: Life & Sex After 50 podcast, says. Lubricants work by reducing friction, which means less risk of irritation or tearing—and just as importantly, more room for pleasure. For best results, we also recommend applying it not just to the penetrating object (like a penis or vibrator) and what’s being penetrated (your vagina), but also during foreplay—for example, consider sliding between labial folds too. (If you’re unsure what lube to buy, start with this beginner-friendly article.)

In some situations, the issue may not be physical or logistical. It’s that the sex you’re having just…isn’t that great.

“If you’re in a relationship or marriage where sex is not exciting, of course you’re not going to want to do it,” Tammy Nelson, PhD, a 63-year-old AASECT-certified sex therapist, who also speaks from personal experience, tells SELF. “It’s like, if the party isn’t fun, why would you go?”

However, one of the many upsides of getting older is acquiring a kind of bluntness your younger self probably shied away from. “At a certain point, you just don’t give a crap,” one 64-year-old woman, speaking anonymously, tells SELF. When you realize life’s too short, you stop worrying so much about how your body looks in certain lighting, how you sound while climaxing, and whether your kinks are “too much.”

“I was once so ashamed to bring up BDSM—being spanked, choked. You don’t want to scare someone off or be judged,” she says. But after years of what she calls “vanilla sex,” she discovered a game-changing truth: speaking up is worth it. “I had my first real orgasm—that I didn’t have to fake—at 61.”

Achieving a mind-blowing climax doesn’t require a partner. For the women SELF spoke with, their 50s and 60s marked a turning point in figuring out what made them squirm—where they enjoyed being touched, what kind of stimulation worked, which fantasies excited them—all thanks to masturbation.

“I feel freer now to explore my body,” Shay Martin, 63, who owns Vibratex (the exclusive distributor of the Magic Wand sex toy brand), tells SELF. “When I was younger, I would use my hands manually, but there are so many tools out there [vibrators, anal toys, penis rings, nipple clamps] to help with achieving an orgasm on your own that’s much more intense and lasts longer.”

Research backs up the benefits of solo play: Not only does masturbation feel great, but it can also boost confidence in your sexuality (something older women are rarely encouraged to embrace) and relieve menopause-related symptoms like vaginal dryness, low sex drive, and mood changes. Once you figure out what feels good, “it becomes a whole lot easier to communicate exactly what you want from another person,” Dr. Nelson says—which makes settling for mediocre hookups (the kind you may have tolerated in your 20s) far less likely.

Bodies in their 60s don’t always cooperate the way they used to—and that’s okay.

An aching back and weak knees have made certain positions uncomfortable for Isma, 68. “Standard missionary can be tough, so I usually lie on my side with my husband spooning behind me,” she tells SELF. (Another option experts previously recommended to SELF includes child’s pose, which can give you better control over the positioning of your back. Or, for pelvic pain, you can hop on top to adjust the depth of penetration and keep it shallow.)

Sometimes, Isma says she uses a wedged, foam pillow under her hips for extra support too. (Yes, there are specialized sex pillows that stay sturdy and don’t flatten out, helping you maintain the right angle without discomfort.) “It’s not as effortless or spontaneous as it used to be,” Isma admits, reflecting on how creating intimacy has changed throughout the years. “But we’ve learned our ways to make it work.”

According to Dr. Nelson, it’s a common misconception that sex is only “good” when it includes penetration and ends in an orgasm. But expanding your definition—not by lowering your standards but by adjusting them—can keep intimacy exciting and realistic.

That might mean focusing on in-the-moment sensations over outcomes: slower pacing, more touch, less pressure to cum. “He genuinely loves going down on me,” Isma says of her husband, describing a nightly, pre-bed ritual that they have maintained almost every day for the past five years. “I don’t usually finish, and neither does he. It just feels amazing. We always look forward to it.”

Martin has found something similar through practicing erotic massages. “At first I was intimidated, because you hear so much about the decline in libido, pain, lack of newness.” Now, Martin says, the slow buildup and warm oil rubbing throughout her erogenous zones is what she anticipates most.

While sex after 60 may not be the kind of stuff that makes it onto racy TV scenes (for now!), that’s precisely what experts say gives it power: It’s a slow, personalized intimacy built only through decades of experimentation, exploration, and curiosity—the kind that only gets better with age.

#8956. Meet AMAA, Neri&Hu’s pick for the most influential architect of the next 20 years

Photography by Mikael Olsson unless stated

An innovative approach to the reuse of existing buildings defines the output of Italian architecture office AMAA, which Neri&Hu has selected as one of 20 names to watch in architecture and design as part of Dezeen’s 20×20 project, sponsored by Kohler.

Led by Marcello Galiotto and Alessandra Rampazzo, over the past 14 years AMAA has become known for its approach to the reuse of post-industrial structures in northern Italy, with the transformation of a former factory building into its own studio, a typical example of its approach.

According to Galiotto, these buildings are a taste of what the studio wants to achieve.

“What we have done in the past 10 years is really just a sketch of what we can do in the future,” he told Dezeen.

“Our research is still growing, and it can be applied to various programmes and contexts,” he continued, “but in 20 years we will both be 60 so we want the studio to be able to evolve and grow in new directions.”

The preservation and adaptation of existing buildings, which is central to AMAA’s practice, is a key reason why architects Lyndon Neri and Rossana Hu selected the studio for Dezeen’s 20×20 series.

“AMAA is significant for its fierce commitment to adaptive reuse,” said the duo, adding that the studio’s ability to repurpose historic structures “positions them as leaders in circular, life-cycle thinking in contemporary Italian architecture”.

AMAA is significant for its fierce commitment to adaptive reuse, [which] positions them as leaders in circular, life-cycle thinking in contemporary Italian architecture

Galiotto and Rampazzo met Neri and Hu when they participated in the 2023 Venice Biennale and have since been invited to host lectures at the University of Pennsylvania, where Hu is chair of the architecture department.

“We have a long relationship with Lyndon and Rossana who we consider to be both amazing people and great architects so it’s truly an honour to be selected by them,” said Galiotto.

Rampazzo added that she saw a clear overlap between Shanghai-based Neri&Hu’s work, which also has a focus on adaptive reuse approach, and their approach at AMAA.

“I’m a fan of their work and I see similarities in the way we do architecture and also the way we teach, despite our different cultural backgrounds,” she said. “I also love how they really support students and young architects by sharing their knowledge. We have a lot to learn from them but I hope we can have the same kind of legacy.”

Rampazzo and Galiotto have known each other for more than 20 years after meeting while studying architecture at the Iuav University of Venice.

The studio now has offices in Venice and in the industrial town of Arzignano, and has gradually become established among Italy’s most respected architecture firms thanks to projects such as their own office and a cafe housed within a 19th-century town hall.

We felt our education hadn’t provide us with knowledge of how to run a medium or large-scale practice, so my experience with Sou Fujimoto was about closing the gap between the present and future of our studio

The pair studied together at Iuav under the professorship of Massimo Carmassi, who they cite as an important influence on their approach to restoration and reuse.

After graduating in 2010, they assisted Carmassi and briefly set up a studio with friends to work on competitions. Then Galiotto went to Japan to work for Sou Fujimoto, while Rampazzo travelled to India for her PhD studies.

“We felt our education hadn’t provide us with knowledge of how to run a medium or large-scale practice,” said Galiotto, “so my experience with Sou Fujimoto was about closing the gap between the present and future of our studio.”

This global travel and work experience helped open their minds to alternative approaches and opportunities, as well as giving them the confidence to set up their own studio back in Venice.

“We’re still evolving, and evolving our identity,” said Galiotto. “But the important thing was to find ourselves. That’s why the path was complicated.

“Stay in Italy… going outside of Italy… travelling the world as much as we can to see things. That was the key, I think, to the position that we are covering right now in the panorama of architecture in Italy.”

In 2015, they opened a branch office in Galiotto’s hometown of Arzignano, which has been described as an “AMAA playground” due to the number of projects the practice has completed there.

Galiotto pointed out that their work in the town is part of an ongoing research into how architecture can blur the line between private and public spaces, with the Caffe Nazionale project providing a good example.

“Although the cafe is privately owned, it also forms the edge of a plaza so we wanted to give the space back to the people,” the architect explained, adding that the studio has coined the term “super public” to describe this aspect of their practice.

Alongside their work in Arzignano and Venice, AMAA now has commissions across Italy, including hospitality and residential projects, as well as schools and a theatre. Along with a focus on reuse, especially industrial buildings, Galiotto believes that the studio’s work is united by its considered eclecticism.

“We’re influenced by art, artists, travels and whatever we can be – by curiosity,” he said. “I would say it’s something that’s very important and it gives us this kind of eclecticism. Our architecture in this moment is very eclectic and at the same time has a strong direction.”

“It’s like a piano symphony, very complicated and very up and down, but at the same time very right like a poem, very well taught and very well executed, but very complicated in terms of ingredients.”

The studio’s expanding list of projects has caused it to swell in size to approximately 30 members of staff, which Galiotto suggested is necessary to facilitate their detailed, research-led approach.

We often collaborate closely with other architects, but we are also influenced by painting, sculpture and photography which enhances the eclecticism of our projects

Looking ahead, the architects said their main objective is to continue developing their team and consolidating their approach so that others can carry it on in the coming decades.

One concern they have is maintaining the same quality of output as demand for their services grows and they take on an increasing number of projects.

In just the past year they have completed 10 projects – as many as they delivered during the first decade of their practice – with public commissions now joining their work for private clients.

Despite the rapid growth, Galiotto and Rampazzo insisted their approach remains consistent whatever scale of project they are working on, whether it’s a chair, a public plaza or a museum, which they both agree would be a dream next project.

Asked for her view on the future of architecture over the coming decades, Rampazzo said there is a trend in Italy towards involving other creatives in the design process, which represents an alternative to the more autocratic approach of the past.

“Sharing ideas and opinions leads to more interesting outcomes,” she claimed. “We often collaborate closely with other architects, but we are also influenced by painting, sculpture and photography which enhances the eclecticism of our projects.”

In their teaching roles at institutions including Kent State University and Universidade do Minho in Portugal, Galiotto and Rampazzo are responsible for helping to shape the attitudes of the next generation of architects, who they recognise are entering the workplace in challenging times.

Galiotto said if there is one thing he tries to pass on to his students and the staff in his studio it is to “have passion and to keep pushing for what you believe in.”

“If you are humble, passionate and curious then you can find success,” he added. “Sometimes it can be tough, but when you love what you do you can live your life feeling like you never worked for a single day.”

To celebrate Dezeen’s 20th birthday, we asked 20 of the most influential architects and designers of the last 20 years to identify someone they think will have a major impact in the next 20 years. Over the next four weeks, we’ll reveal their picks in a series of profile interviews.

#8955. Pucker Up! How to Heal Cracked Lip Corners Fast

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

Smiling for selfies should be fun, not painful! If cracked lip corners or angular cheilitis make it hard to smile, eat, or kiss, don’t worry. Check out these tips to heal those cracks quickly. With some care and good habits, you’ll have pain-free, makeout-ready lips in no time. Say goodbye to angular cheilitis and hello to a happier smile!

The first step to healing your cracked lip corners quickly is to lock in any moisture. Reach for a product dermatologists call an occlusive, which creates a protective barrier that prevents your lip corners from getting drier. Vaseline, Aquafor, or CeraVe ointment are common occlusives that will help reduce cracking.

Dab a little coconut oil, olive oil, or fragrance-free moisturizer on the corners of your lips daily after you shower. Make it a daily habit, but don’t go overboard. A little dab will do. Allow your skin’s natural oils to build back up as the cracking fades. Bonus tip: Add the occlusive lip barrier after moisturizing.

Locking in moisture only works if you have enough moisture, so staying hydrated is key! Keep a refillable water bottle with you as your trusty sidekick. Sip on plain water throughout the day, or jazz it up with a splash of cucumber or another non-acidic flavor. Pro tip: Avoid lemon juice, which can irritate and sting sensitive skin.

Bonus: Staying hydrated will help your raw lip corners heal quicker and improve your skin’s overall health.

Have you noticed that moisture is a common theme here? Lend your lips a humid hand by sleeping with a humidifier beside your bed. Adding moisture to the air is especially helpful for your cracked lips during the winter or in hot, dry climates. Think about popping a small humidifier in your workspace or wherever you spend the most time.

It might seem like a quick fix to lick your lips to keep them moist, but that can make things worse. Saliva evaporates quickly, leaving a sticky residue that can attract bacteria and lead to infection. So, keep your tongue away from your lips and remember this: “Licking your lips will cause them to lickety-split.”

Whether from frigid cold or dry heat, your skin can lose water rapidly, causing cracking, flaking, discoloration, or swelling. So avoid jumping from a sweltering afternoon at the beach into a freezing cold movie theater.

Also, skip the hot showers or cold plunges for a bit. These types of rapid temperature changes will quickly dry out your lip corners. Bonus tip: Your lips can take a beating from the sun, so find a lip balm with SPF protection.

If your cracked lip corners don’t improve or become especially painful or swollen in a few days, it’s time to visit a board-certified dermatologist. If left untreated, angular cheilitis can last for years, leaving your lips discolored or scarred.

FYI: Angular cheilitis might not appear as clearly in people with darker skin. Instead of turning red, the affected skin may look pale and have a darker border.

Remember that lickety-split mantra? It’s for real. Saliva can get deposited in the corners of your lips for many reasons, like drooling, smoking, or sleeping with your mouth open due to some sniffles. Bacteria grows in those little saliva pools, triggering an inflammatory response that causes your lip corners to get irritated and crack.

Following these tips will make your lips feel better in about a week. Really bad cases of angular cheilitis can take a few weeks. Avoid smoking and eat a balanced diet to get faster results.

As mentioned above, Vaseline and other occlusives help create a protective barrier over the cracked lip corners, which helps the healing process.

You might have woken up with cracked lip corners, but you won’t be able to get rid of them overnight. Be patient and follow the tips above!

Say goodbye to painful cracked lip corners in about a week with these easy tips:

Talk to a dermatologist for customized care if your lip corners become red, swollen, or more painful after a few days.
